nodes.t: Beijing demands Mitsurugi's newest capacitor
nodes.x: Beijing asked Mitsurugi for a Mk.III licence and was told the core didn't exist. A week later, Beijing's customs began holding Japanese capacitor shipments at every port on the Chinese coast. Mitsurugi's board quietly registered subsidiaries in Vladivostok and Ohio and began copying its design archives to both. Licence Diplomacy was built for a world where nobody wanted the factory more than the parts.

nodes.t: Japan falls into China's sphere
nodes.x: Projected. Beijing never lands an army on the home islands. It doesn't need to: the ports already run on Tianshu's schedule, the grain still comes on credit, and when the Pacific war starts the Kansai government asks for protection. Chinese liaison officers arrive at JSDF headquarters within the month, and Japan ends the war inside China's sphere. Not all of Mitsurugi goes with it: the subsidiaries in Vladivostok and Ohio take engineers, archives and actuator lines with them. The line that leaves through Russia will go a long way further.

nodes.t: A Russian advance across the Bering Strait
nodes.x: Projected. The Russian half of the Pact Civil War carries its fight across the Bering Strait, and the United States, with little left to stop it, answers with atomic weapons. The limited exchange across the northern front destroys Vancouver. Luna's fleets end the war soon after.

nodes.t: From the Spratly reef to Australia
nodes.x: Projected. The Tieshan-Kai company Tianshu set down on a Spratly reef in 2178 turns out to be the first of many. Chinese landings spread through the Philippines and Indonesia, and American carriers fall back on Australia to hold the line.

nodes.t: Vireo's hidden halls burn, and nobody knows what got out
nodes.x: Projected. On the Oceania Front, a single air raid nobody claims burns the pump works on the Makassar waterfront. The firefighters find what the pumps were hiding: three floors of server halls dug into the reclaimed land beneath them, cooled by the harbour and running until the fire reached them. It burns for three days. No bodies are ever counted, because there were never any bodies there. Vireo's shell companies go silent the same week, yet continuity contracts out in the Belt go on being honoured for decades, by somebody. Whether the recordings were inside, copied out in time, or never there at all, nobody outside ███████ knows.

nodes.t: The first crewed Mars landing
nodes.x: Not a conflict. It belongs here because Station Nine, Colony One and the Melas Landing all trace back to ████ ███ ████ ████ █████.

nodes.t: Ascension workers vs station security
nodes.x: The first station labour dispute. Workers armed Lifter frames with rivet drivers and torches and held a station for a month. Ascension settled, and never fully disarmed them.

nodes.t: The lunar towns get councils
nodes.x: By the 2170s Ascension's ice towns at the lunar poles held more people than any station, and the first children born on the Moon were starting school. Rather than face a second Rivet Strike a long way from any security frame, the board gave Shackleton, Malapert, Peary and the old landing city at Tranquility a charter: elected councils, and seats on the yard board. The bloc shareholders signed it without reading closely, because the Moon was a mining camp.

nodes.t: Bloc teams fight over a drifting cargo pod
nodes.x: Boarding teams from two blocs reached the same derelict cargo pod near the elevator, and Rigger Security frames fought with harpoons and spike drivers. Three people died, the first combat deaths in orbit. Within months, the blocs had commissioned the first dedicated warships.

nodes.t: A treaty to keep orbit unarmed, vetoed by every bloc
nodes.x: Weeks after the Tether Incident, the UN tabled a treaty to keep orbit unarmed: no warships, no armed frames above the atmosphere, and no reactor-lifted craft in Earth's sky. Each bloc vetoed it, and each commissioned its first warships within months. In the lunar yard someone printed the draft and pinned it up in the crew mess, where it stayed through every bloc's contract. Its third clause becomes the Lunar Mandate's first rule.

nodes.t: A sealed station goes dark for nine hours
nodes.x: Station Nine lost contact for nine hours, the same week Halden activated H-17 in Geneva. Ascension's report blamed a solar flare. There was no flare.

nodes.t: Ascension's lunar half merges with the cities and declares a state
nodes.x: Ascension's board had been deadlocked by its bloc shareholders for a decade. In 2182, while the blocs were still dealing with the fallout of Svalbard, the Hari River and the Delhi Accession, its lunar directors voted to merge their half of the consortium with the lunar councils, and the Assembly at Shackleton declared the Lunar Republic. The yards, the ice and the lunar stations became the property of a state, and their crews its citizens. What was left of Ascension didn't last the year: the Republic took the solar ring and the orbital stations its crews already ran, and the bloc shareholders divided the elevators between them. The blocs called it theft, then remembered who would be building their warships, and started calling it a jurisdictional question. The Republic's first act was to apply to join the UN. The Council vetoed it, and the Assembly seated it as an observer. From every window in the Republic, Earth hangs in the same place in the sky, and every year it is a little browner.

nodes.t: The first permanent settlement on another planet
nodes.x: The second Mars mission, which Washington took over when Ascension was broken up, was a settlement, not a landing. Its settlers needed radiation-hardening gene therapy, and US law bars enhanced citizens from federal service, so the Americans among them resigned their commissions and went as civilians on the mission's contract. This year they landed and named their settlement Colony One: the first permanent human home on another planet. Washington insisted on a written charter guaranteeing its oversight, and the settlers are already arguing over the clauses. Their leader is one of the two Ares crew who never gave another interview.

nodes.t: Tianlong's prospecting families keep their own books
nodes.x: Tianlong's orbital subsidiary sent family-crewed tenders out to prospect near-Earth asteroids. Out there, Tianshu's plans arrive late and fit badly, so the crews keep their own ledgers, trade among themselves and settle disputes by reputation. Beijing calls them contractors. They have started calling themselves houses.

nodes.t: Warships in orbit, no doctrine to use them
nodes.x: The first dedicated warships carry mass drivers and Marlinspike frames on their catapults. Nobody has fought with them yet. Every one of them came off the Lunar Republic's slipway.

nodes.t: Every bloc's first warships, built in a slipway none of them owns
nodes.x: When the Tether Incident sent every bloc looking for warships, only one yard could build them: the Lunar Republic's slipway on the rim of Shackleton crater. No bloc wants to depend on a state on the Moon, so each has started building its own way up, but in 2186 every bloc's first warships still come off the lunar slipway. Nothing on Earth matches what it makes: hulls cast in vacuum, composites cured in the cold of the crater floor, coil drivers machined in one piece. The Republic sells the hulls to every bloc and gives the best of what it makes to the UN. Among themselves, its engineers no longer say Ascension. They say lunar.

nodes.t: An unannounced settlement on ███ ████ █████ ███ ████████ ███
nodes.x: Months after Colony One, a lander in Ascension's old livery came down in Melas Chasma, in the middle of Valles Marineris, on top of ███ ████ █████ ███ ████ ████ █████ ███ ████████. Its manifest called it a Colony One survey camp; nobody asked Colony One. Its crew came from Station Nine, and they are digging for ████████. Halden's scientists, drafting a proposal for a supervised station in the same canyon, don't know one is already there. When Mars is divided, the Red Line between north and south will run straight across it.

nodes.t: The Republic's cold war goes hot in its own domes
nodes.x: The Republic's politics split two ways, and every bloc pays someone. The Earthward, strongest in the yards, hold that Luna exists for Earth, because space is dark and cold without it, and want the Republic in the UN. The Farsiders, mostly young and lunar-born, say Earth is finished and Luna should sell its warships to the highest bidder and close the door. In 2185 it went hot. A pressure seal at Malapert failed during a Farsider rally and killed forty-one people. The next week a bloc trade office at Peary had its air cut, and a Speaker was shot on the Assembly floor. Nobody has proved who opened the seal. The answer was emergency law: the yard militias became the Lunar Guard, the blocs' advisers were sent home, and the Farsider leaders went to the far-side ice camps. First Speaker Teodora Halloran kept the Earthward policy and took the Farsiders' methods, and the Republic is a harder place than it was a year ago.

nodes.t: Every bloc builds its own way into orbit
nodes.x: No bloc will trust its navy to a state on the Moon, so each is building its own way up. The Pact builds hull sections on the ground and throws them into orbit on the Tian Shan Rail, a magnetic track up the mountains on the Kazakh–Kyrgyz border; both of its General Staffs claim it. The Union has leased docks of its own on Malapert Mountain, inside the Republic, and argues with the Lunar Guard about who inspects them. The United States is building the Hampton Roads Orbital Dockyard at the L1 point, named for the Navy yard the sea took. In 2186 all three are behind schedule, and every first warship still comes off the lunar slipway. But when Luna closes the lanes, none of them will be locked out of space.

nodes.t: The first war fought between ships
nodes.x: Projected. The warships nobody knew how to use learn fast. Fleets fight over the elevators, the solar ring and the lanes to the Moon, and the carriers find that frames win boarding actions but are too slow for open space, so they launch fighter craft beside them. At the Battle of Yernon a single British dreadnought breaks the Russian inner fleet, and a Union written off since the European Front is a great power again. The lunar yards build for every side, the Tian Shan Rail and Hampton Roads build for their own, and the Republic watches.

nodes.t: The Lunar Republic puts its fleets under the UN, and the war stops
nodes.x: Projected. By its last year the war has pushed a biosphere already damaged by two centuries of warming close to collapse, and the atomic exchange over the northern front nearly finishes it. The Lunar Republic, hardened by Tranquility, refuses to launch for any bloc. It places the yards, the ring and every ship it crews under the United Nations, the one institution every side had ignored through the war and still let into the ruins, and closes the lanes down to Earth until the blocs stop fighting. Each bloc keeps a road to orbit, rebuilt or reopened under UN inspection: the Tian Shan Rail, wrecked in the war, is relaid, and the Malapert docks and Hampton Roads go back to work. That is the main reason the blocs accept it. Its first rule is the third clause of the treaty every bloc vetoed in 2184: nothing lifted by a reactor flies over Earth again. It ends the war and founds the United Nations of Earth and Luna: an institution with its own navy and a mandate to protect humanity from itself, which few asked for and none could refuse. The Republic's Assembly sits on as UNEL's lunar chamber, and its Guard crews the Luna half of the fleet.

nodes.t: Farsiders seize a lunar city, and the Republic hardens
nodes.x: Projected. Midway through the war, Farsider cells seize Tranquility, the old near-side landing city, and offer the Republic's slipways to whichever bloc will recognise them. At least two blocs answer. The Lunar Guard retakes the city in nine days, dome by dome, with the Custodian walking through the breaches. After that the Republic stops pretending to be neutral about anything. The leadership that comes out of Tranquility is the one that refuses to launch for any bloc, closes the lanes, and hands its fleets to the UN on its own terms.

nodes.t: Horn raid bands vs India's west coast
nodes.x: Raid bands from the Horn and the Yemeni coast began crossing the Arabian Sea on the monsoon wind, in dhow-ferries with a rebuilt Garrison or Tieniu lying on the deck. They hit Gujarat's ports and the Konkan fuel depots and were gone before the Indian Army's tanks arrived. India had no frames: its licence requests were still waiting in Washington and Beijing. Doctors who examined captured raiders found bone and muscle therapies made for Ascension's low-gravity crews, pirated by the free-port clinics of the Horn. Raiders who should have died walked back to their boats. They were the first enhanced soldiers anyone fought, and India fought them alone.

nodes.t: Monsoon bands burn India's largest oil port
nodes.x: The monsoon bands came back with Haboobs. Twelve frames landed at night, held Kandla for six hours and burned it. The company of Tieshan-Is that Delhi had bought from Beijing arrived from Ahmedabad on the second day, three frames short: their actuator spares were in a Tianlong depot, waiting for Tianshu to schedule them. Delhi asked Washington for frames once more and was offered a licence on the terms Ottawa had been paying for a decade. A year later many of the same bands rode in the Convoy Raids, and started calling themselves League.

nodes.t: The Commonwealth catches the raid cadres at last
nodes.x: Projected. For thirty years the raid cadres were someone else's problem: India's, then the blocs', then the League's own embarrassment. By the last year of the war the African Union has frames of its own design, battalions that know the coast and nothing left to be embarrassed about. It runs the cadres down from the Ogaden to the Horn and corners them at Ras Hafun, where the first bands set out for India. It does not execute them. It puts them aboard hulls bought from the lunar yards, the first ships it ever paid for, and lets any grafted soldier who chooses to follow them go too. Some of those who choose are its own veterans. The ships go to Jupiter, and the Commonwealth's first law about space is that they don't come back.

nodes.t: The Pact vs India on the Ladakh heights
nodes.x: A Tianlong road crew reached a pass that India claimed, with a company of Tieniu kneeling on the ridge above it. India had tanks that couldn't climb to them and no frames at all. After a month Delhi withdrew its posts and called it a negotiated adjustment; Beijing called it a road. Indian newspapers printed the photograph of a kneeling Tieniu on that ridge for years, under different headlines, and a generation of Indian officers still measure how far India fell behind by it.

nodes.t: The Steppe splits between protection and the Belt
nodes.x: Projected. In the first winter of the Pact Civil War the Steppe camps hold an assembly at Darkhan. Beijing offers what the steppe has always needed and seldom had: protection, rail and a place in the plan. The price is the plan. The camps split. Most take the protection, guard Beijing's railheads for the rest of the war, and their grandchildren still run the Ground to Orbit Accelerator. The rest, the wind riders who never let Tianshu route them and most of Khiimori's younger members, load what they can carry onto the last launches up the Tian Shan Rail before it is wrecked, and join the prospecting houses in the Belt. Each half says the other sold the horse.

nodes.t: The Ascendancy sends its oath-sworn pilots away
nodes.x: Projected. By the end of the war Moscow and Delhi know what the next one will look like: Jingweis that answer only to a network, grafted raiders who won't die and, in their own sealed files, the Koschei. They agree on little, but they agree that someone will have to hunt that kind of thing, and that it should be people who can't be made into it. The Nashik pilots won't be commanded by anyone who ran Department Zero, and say so. So at Vladivostok, beside the grounded Hakobune, envoys from both capitals hand them the ship, the Ashvin drawings and the Mitsurugi exiles who asked to go with them, with a blessing the Compact still recites: you won't let us control you; you have our blessing; now leave, before we change our minds.

nodes.t: Washington's allies pay for its carriers
nodes.x: Not a conflict. When drowned coasts and failing harvests made America's carrier fleet too expensive even for America, Washington asked its North Atlantic allies to pay for their protection by the tonne. Canada paid in Quebec hydrogen at Washington's price, Norway and Iceland in seabed and basing rights, and Britain in its last shipyards' order books. The compact is renewed every ten years. Each renewal costs more, and nobody in Ottawa, London, Oslo or Reykjavik can say what the last one bought.

nodes.t: Washington forbids Britain a Union frame
nodes.x: The British Army wanted the Union's Haubert, whose hardpoints took any weapon its crews could find. Washington's answer came from Halcyon, not the State Department: if one Haubert crossed the Channel, Halcyon would stop servicing Britain's Kestrels. Britain kept the Kestrel and paid for the privilege under the Burden Share. The Ministry of Defence also kept the Union's offer letter, framed, in a corridor every new minister has to walk down.

nodes.t: Britain is refused a slipway of its own
nodes.x: Britain offered to pay a third of the Hampton Roads Orbital Dockyard in return for one berth of its own. Washington offered the Clyde's shipwrights jobs at L1 building American hulls, and the Royal Navy the right to crew a few of them. In March the Admiralty asked Strasbourg, quietly, whether the Malapert docks had room. The Union's council, which has never agreed on anything quickly, agreed in nine days. Britain's first orbital hull is laid down on the Moon under a Union lease, and it will be a dreadnought.

nodes.t: Both sides start stocking a line nobody has drawn
nodes.x: After the Halifax Motion, people on both sides start stocking a line nobody has drawn yet. In the autumn the RCMP finds two depots outside Kenora, forty kilometres apart: one full of Brannock-Hale actuator spares consigned to a heritage rifle club in Winnipeg, the other full of Union reformer stacks consigned to a Montreal hydro cooperative. Neither owner is charged. Both depots are restocked within the month, and Boreal's Wolverine order book has two customers it can't name.

nodes.t: Canadians fight Canadians across the Shield
nodes.x: Projected. The partition line doesn't hold still. Through the first two winters it is fought across the Shield forests and frozen lakes between Lake Superior and Hudson Bay, by Canadians in Canadian frames on both sides: Calgary's Wolverines against Montreal's, Tundras dug out of reserve depots, and Polaris rescue frames that both sides stop pretending are unarmed. Washington supplies the west and Strasbourg the east, and both treat it as the cheapest front of the war. It isn't cheap for the people who live on it. Small units lie in the snow for days and strike at the supply roads, and towns change hands at forty below. Each half of the Aurora is seen on the line at least once.

nodes.t: A million people carried onto the ice
nodes.x: Projected. When the Winter War reaches the towns, Ottawa and Edmonton both run evacuations, and then neither can. Ice-road haulers, Polaris frames and a frozen-in Union Polar Carrier move a million people north along the old mining roads into the Arctic archipelago, to wait out the war where nobody fights. Most never come south again. Their camps at Resolute, Alert and Thule are where the Polar Exodus begins, and some of their children will leave Earth from the ice without ever having lived anywhere warm.

nodes.t: Forty-one votes against Unaltered Crews, and a charter nobody reads
nodes.x: When Unaltered Crews became regulation, forty-one members of Congress signed a minority report against it. Their case was narrow: a radiation therapy is medicine, not alteration, and a country that bars its own settlers from service will lose them. They lost the vote and stayed in government: liberals from the coasts and the border states who believed in the state they were arguing with. “We lose votes. We don't lose the country.” Their appendix was a model charter for American territory off Earth: an elected assembly, a bill of rights covering every settler, altered or not, and war powers kept in Washington, so that no colony could ever start a war in America's name. Washington took the oversight clauses for Colony One's charter and shelved the rest.

nodes.t: Beijing feeds Japan, and Tianshu learns its ports
nodes.x: Two failed harvests in a row left Japan buying rice, and only Beijing had rice to sell. It came on credit, secured against the port fees at Hakata, Kobe and Niigata, on Tianlong ships that Tianshu scheduled. Within a year Tianshu was scheduling the ports as well, because it was the only system that knew when the ships would arrive. Tokyo called it an efficiency. The JSDF noticed that Beijing now knew the movements of every ship in Japan's three busiest harbours before Japan's own navy did.

nodes.t: A government elected to settle with Beijing
nodes.x: After the Osaka customs holds, a coalition of exporters, port cities and the grain-debt committees takes the Diet's lower house on a promise to settle with Beijing. Its first bill moves capacitor export licences from the trade ministry to a joint commission with a Chinese co-chair. Its second puts the Tsukuyomi Lab's budget under review. Mitsurugi's board read the second bill and booked flights to Vladivostok.

nodes.t: Colony One recruits people who can go without
nodes.x: The second Mars mission needed settlers who could live on a ration of air, and who would take a gene therapy that ended any federal career. Its recruiters went where people had already stopped waiting for help: stilt towns on the drowned Gulf coast, Alaskan homesteads, desert water communes, the families who ran the Arctic ice roads. The roster asked three questions: can you fix what keeps you alive, can you go without, and will you stay. Washington paid for the mission and never read the roster. Colony One's founders are on it, and so is everyone who later decided Washington's charter was a suggestion.

nodes.t: Elevator berths for people leaving a failing planet
nodes.x: After a third bad harvest year, the elevators' new bloc owners start selling berths to the stations and the Moon to anyone who can pay, and running a lottery for those who can't. The queue grows faster than the berths. The Lunar Republic takes a quota, the stations take whoever has a trade, and the prospecting houses take whole families. Every government on Earth calls it a brain drain, and none of them can stop it without admitting why people want to go.

nodes.t: The Union's ethics panel turns to everything beyond the Moon
nodes.x: Projected. With the European Front burning, the Union's ethics panel holds its hearings in a bunker under Strasbourg rules for its Mars station against the council, and stops asking only what Europe may build. Its four hundred pages on a station on Mars become a question about everything beyond the Moon: who may be changed out there, what may be grown, and who answers for it. The panel decides that someone must, and that it had better be people who have read the conditions. That decision is the founding charter of the Martian Research Directorate.

nodes.t: Every front sends people up
nodes.x: Projected. The war empties more than cities. Every front sends people up, on whatever is flying: refugees on returning ore carriers, crews who desert with their ships, engineers sold passage by their own governments to keep them out of enemy hands. They go to the Moon, to the Belt houses, to Mars on both sides of the line that will divide it, and as far out as anyone will carry them. Every space power of the next century is built by people who left in the war, and most of them never tell their children what they left behind.

nodes.t: Mexican water engineers sign on for Colony One's first resupply
nodes.x: Colony One's settlers know how to go without. None of them knows how to share. The mission's resupply recruiters went to the river commission set up by the Rio Bravo Compact, whose Mexican engineers and water judges had spent five years dividing a shrinking river by law and getting both banks to accept the rulings. As Mexican citizens they could take the radiation therapy without giving up a career, and forty families are on the manifest for the first resupply flight. They bring court-kept water ledgers with the Virgin of Guadalupe painted on the covers, and the habit of settling an argument before anyone reaches for a weapon. When Mexico joins the United States in the war, they become, overnight, enhanced American citizens whom no law yet covers.

nodes.t: Beijing makes the houses its clients
nodes.x: Tianshu's Belt forecast finds that the prospecting houses bring home more ore when it leaves them alone than when it routes them, and Beijing does what the network advises. Instead of disciplining the houses, the Ministry of Commerce charters them. They get a Chinese registry, Chinese insurance, refits in Tianlong's orbital docks and the protection of the flag. Beijing gets first refusal on every cargo sold through the new exchange at Juno, and a copy of every survey. The charter needs a name, so a clerk gives it one: the Celestial Prosperity Syndicate. The houses laugh at it, then paint it on their hulls, because no other navy will board a ship carrying a name Beijing wrote. Beijing calls it patronage. The houses call it a contract, and read the termination clauses first.

nodes.t: Beijing's Belt ships pass to the Syndicate
nodes.x: Projected. When the Pact Civil War calls Beijing's ships home, it cannot hold the Belt and fight in Central Asia at once. So it leases what it has out there to the Syndicate for the duration: survey tenders, armed haulers, the first Steppe corvettes, and a carrier no house could ever have bought. The terms are simple. The houses keep the hulls flying, and China's ore keeps coming home at cost. The convoys do not miss a delivery in the whole war, and Syndicate arbiters still bring that up in every negotiation with Beijing. Nobody ever closes the lease. Beijing never asks for the ships back, the Syndicate never stops shipping at a discount, and both find the debt more useful than a settlement. The Chinese hulls still flying for the Syndicate in 2327 came to it the same way, and so did the habit: Beijing builds, the Syndicate flies.

nodes.t: Mars refuses an order from Europe
nodes.x: Projected. In the war's second year, with the European Front breaking, the Union's council orders its new station on Mars to do what the panel forbade: grow tissue, harden soldiers and ship the results home. The station is run by Halden's surviving scientists, the people disgraced for doing exactly that. Their director answers with the page of the conditions that allows no wartime exception, and refuses. Strasbourg cuts off the station's supply. The crew ration air, buy spares from Colony One's settlers, who think them fools, and make the rest themselves. When the panel hears the case in its bunker, it rules for the station against the council that created it. Nobody on Mars forgets that Europe asked, and nobody in Strasbourg forgets that Mars said no. It is the first time the station's crew sign their reports as a directorate.

weapons.label: Weapons
weapons.intro: Mech weapons began as vehicle guns, missiles and construction tools strapped onto walking frames. Two generations later, every bloc has its own branch, and the energy weapons at the end of each branch barely work. Not everything here fires: by 2186 the deadliest weapons in some lances are a jammer, a datalink and a shield.
turns: The first mech gun was an IFV cannon with a grip. Within five years every bloc fielded a licensed or stolen copy, which is why Gen 2 and Gen 3 mounts worldwide are still sized for it.
Shoulder-mounted tank guns could topple a frame that fired outside its kneeling envelope. Bracing became doctrine, and Pact heavy weapons are still built to fire from a kneel.
Every linear and energy weapon in service traces back to MHI capacitor tech, whether licensed, bought or stolen. Japan's neutrality holds because every bloc depends on it.
Directive 5 made the Union's jammers its first weapon. By Gen 3 Funkenwerk was building them from public drawings, and Beijing had answered the other way: a network that aims for you.
The BX-0 fires five shots, then cools for ninety seconds. The plasma blade lasts forty seconds. The Iskra needs a truck. Whoever solves power wins Gen 4.
fams: The workhorse. Every bloc's main gun descends from one US design.
Tank guns that learned to walk. The Pact's speciality.
Infantry and artillery munitions moved onto mechs, from two tubes to forty-rocket salvos.
Construction tools, blades and lances. Where bloc styles differ most.
Railguns and coilguns. A US advantage built on Mitsurugi parts.
Prototypes or defence-only. Nothing here is reliable yet.
Weapons that hit nothing directly. The Union blinds first; Beijing lets a network aim.
Ascension construction equipment, slowly being turned into weapons.

nodes.t: IFV turrets and aircraft gun pods
nodes.x: Chain guns and revolver cannons from infantry fighting vehicles and ground-attack aircraft. Proven, plentiful, and the obvious first thing to hand a mech.

nodes.t: An IFV gun with a pistol grip
nodes.x: The first mech-portable gun to see combat. Brannock-Hale took a stock 30 mm chain gun, added a grip, a shoulder brace and a 120-round box, and shipped it. Crude, but it worked, and every bloc copied it within five years.

nodes.t: 40 mm with underbarrel grenade launcher
nodes.x: The US Army's standard rifle. A bigger round to beat Gen 2 armour, plus a 60 mm underbarrel launcher for bunkers. Rugged enough to use as a club, and pilots do.

nodes.t: Compact 35 mm ammo, programmable airburst
nodes.x: VEK licence-built the M30 as the G30, then replaced it. The G35 fires cased-telescoped rounds that burst on command, cued by VEK's sensor suite. Excellent and expensive; supply officers hate the ammunition chain. Funkenwerk's runners carry it because its drawings are public, and in 2186 the Tsagaan Salkhi carried it into the Pact.

nodes.t: Reverse-engineered M30, looser tolerances
nodes.x: Built from M30s captured in a border clash. Tianlong loosened every tolerance and added a 200-round drum. Less accurate than the original, and it keeps firing when caked in mud. Every Pact depot stocks its drums, which is why Khiimori's Takhi and Bürged carry it.

nodes.t: The Strizh's gun, built into an arm
nodes.x: OKB-7 took the twin-barrel 30 mm cannon out of the Strizh and built it into the Korsak's right forearm, belt-fed from a magazine in the upper arm. There was never a hand-held version, and that habit later gave the Medved its rotary cannons.

nodes.t: Aircraft gatling built into the arm
nodes.x: OKB-7 skipped the hand-held stage and built an aircraft rotary cannon straight into the forearm. Huge rate of fire, short range, and a frame that can't drop its gun when it runs dry.

nodes.t: Type-07 action, M30 barrel, VEK sight
nodes.x: The League's standard rifle is three rivals' parts on one gun: a licensed Type-07 action, surplus M30 barrels and second-hand VEK optics. Spares are interchangeable with half the black market.

nodes.t: Capacitor-ignited plasma propellant
nodes.x: A bridge between chemical and linear guns: a capacitor pulse turns the propellant into plasma for much higher velocity. The Army licensed its capacitors from Mitsurugi rather than depend on Halcyon. In field trials.

nodes.t: Main battle tank guns
nodes.x: Standard MBT main guns. Enormous recoil, designed to be absorbed by a fifty-tonne hull, not a walking frame.

nodes.t: Light, single-shot anti-tank tubes
nodes.x: Shoulder-fired recoilless rifles. No recoil, big back-blast, cheap to make.

nodes.t: A tank gun bolted to the shoulder
nodes.x: Tianlong's first answer to armour: a whole tank gun on the shoulder. Its safe firing envelope required a kneel, and crews who fired standing could be thrown off their feet. Kneeling and bracing became drill, and then doctrine.

nodes.t: Single-shot, hand-reloaded
nodes.x: America's lighter answer: a scaled-up recoilless rifle. No recoil, a huge back-blast, and the pilot reloads one shell at a time by hand.

nodes.t: 200 mm, hand-carried, folding bipod
nodes.x: The signature Pact weapon. A 200 mm smoothbore carried two-handed, with a folding bipod and a massive muzzle brake. Fired from a kneel at ranges where rifles can't reply.

nodes.t: Rocket-assisted, five-round clip
nodes.x: The M105 grown up: rocket-assisted rounds and a five-round clip. America's main heavy anti-armour weapon, carried in every Brannock fire team.

nodes.t: 152 mm, four-round autoloader
nodes.x: OKB-7 took the Type-09 concept and added a four-round autoloader, so heavy frames can keep firing while they advance. Too heavy for anything but an OKB-7 chassis.

nodes.t: Surplus Type-01 with mining-rig dampers
nodes.x: The League bought retired Type-01s by the hundred and added hydraulic recoil dampers taken from mining rigs. League frames can fire them standing, something Tianlong never managed.

nodes.t: 305 mm, fired from an anchored frame
nodes.x: A siege weapon for OKB-7's new breakthrough frames. The firing mech drives spades into the ground to anchor itself, and a second mech carries the ammunition.

nodes.t: Infantry and vehicle ATGMs
nodes.x: Wire- and laser-guided anti-tank missiles. The shaped-charge warhead technology later spread well beyond missiles.

nodes.t: Truck-mounted artillery rockets
nodes.x: Area-saturation rocket artillery. Cheap per round and terrifying in volume.

nodes.t: Two infantry missiles on the shoulders
nodes.x: Two standard ATGM tubes strapped to a Gen 1 frame. One shot each, but the first sign that mechs could replace tank destroyers.

nodes.t: Sixteen unguided 80 mm rockets
nodes.x: Unguided rockets in a cheap rack. Inaccurate alone, but a company firing together hits something.

nodes.t: 12 cells: anti-armour, anti-air or smoke
nodes.x: A twelve-cell shoulder pod that takes anti-armour, anti-air or smoke missiles. Gen 2 and Gen 3 mounts everywhere are sized for it.

nodes.t: Fighter missiles on the transforming wings
nodes.x: Halcyon kept its fighter heritage: standard air-to-ground and air-to-air missiles carried on the wing binders and fired in flight mode before landing.

nodes.t: Forty rockets in one salvo
nodes.x: The rocket rack taken to its extreme: forty rockets in a back-mounted battery, emptied in a single salvo, then jettisoned. Every Pact breakthrough opens with one.

nodes.t: Fewer cells, seekers that hunt jammers
nodes.x: A licence-built Hornet with VEK seekers that home on enemy jammers. Fewer cells, a far higher hit rate, and the reason US electronic-warfare pilots fear Continental squadrons. Funkenwerk's Querschläger and Aufbruch made it a raider's weapon.

nodes.t: Hornet casing, Pact rockets
nodes.x: A copied Hornet casing loaded with cheap Type-03-pattern rockets. It fits US mounts and takes Eurasian ammunition, so League units can buy from whichever bloc is selling.

nodes.t: Hydraulic construction tools
nodes.x: Hydraulic rams and breakers from demolition and heavy construction.

nodes.t: Industrial blades and saws
nodes.x: Heavy cutting tools from forestry and mining machinery.

nodes.t: Hydraulic stake on the forearm
nodes.x: A demolition ram turned weapon: a hydraulic steel stake that punches through armour at contact range. Slow to cycle, devastating on a hit.

nodes.t: Sharpened plate steel
nodes.x: Plate steel with one sharpened edge. It needs no ammunition, which mattered to an army that couldn't count on resupply.

nodes.t: Explosive-driven, six-shot cylinder
nodes.x: The hydraulics are replaced by explosive blanks in a six-shot cylinder, each one firing the stake. Brannock pilots are close to religious about it.

nodes.t: Shaped-charge tip on a 12 m shaft
nodes.x: A cavalry lance with a missile's shaped-charge warhead in the tip. Paired with the VEK shield it gives Continental mechs their knightly look. Each tip works once.

nodes.t: Layered composite that holds an edge
nodes.x: Layered carbon composite that is lighter and harder than steel and keeps its edge after cutting armour. Cheap to mass-produce, and the Pact's most exported weapon.

nodes.t: High-frequency vibrating edge
nodes.x: Mitsurugi's actuator expertise applied to cutting. The edge vibrates at ultrasonic frequency and saws through armour. It uses a lot of power and wears out quickly.

nodes.t: Mamont right-arm steel hammer
nodes.x: One enormous double-faced steel hammerhead replaces the right hand. Reinforced shoulder and elbow joints swing the maul clear of the chest armour to break concrete barriers.

nodes.t: Licensed HF-1 that stows in the forearm
nodes.x: A shortened, licensed HF-1 that folds into the forearm so it doesn't snag in flight mode. The Kestrel pilot's last resort.

nodes.t: Orbital cutting torch plus MHI capacitors
nodes.x: Castellani combined an Ascension hull-cutting torch with licensed Mitsurugi capacitor cores to make a blade of contained plasma. About forty seconds per charge. The only working unit is assigned to the Union's top ace.

nodes.t: A dozer blade wide enough to cover a family
nodes.x: Qadira's Khartoum office built the first weapon of Protect First, which is mostly a wall: a dozer blade on a shield arm, wide enough to cover a family behind a frame and strong enough to dig them a trench. The Harmattan carries it, the Elissa a lighter one, and the white squads' Albedo cuts firebreaks with a lunar-built copy.

nodes.t: US Navy test guns
nodes.x: Ship-mounted railgun trials that never quite entered service. Barrels eroded fast and needed a destroyer's power plant.

nodes.t: Built for maglev and factory power
nodes.x: Before mechs, Mitsurugi built high-density capacitor banks for maglev lines and heavy industry. That product line turned out to be the key to every energy weapon since.

nodes.t: Tethered to a backpack capacitor
nodes.x: The first mech railgun. Power ran through a tether from a backpack capacitor, eight shots per charge. Accurate, and decisive in the battle where it debuted.

nodes.t: Standard Kestrel armament, MHI core
nodes.x: An MHI capacitor core inside the stock removed the tether. Thirty shots per battery pack, and the hypervelocity rounds go through Gen 2 armour easily. America's main technological edge.

nodes.t: Shorter, slower, far more reliable
nodes.x: Mitsurugi's own design. Lower velocity than the LR-3 but much more reliable, and the capacitor core inside it is the most licensed component in the world.

nodes.t: Built from stolen LR-1 plans
nodes.x: Built from LR-1 plans obtained through espionage. It works, but barrel erosion forces a change every forty shots. Issued only to elite Pact units.

nodes.t: Long-range, limited by fuel-cell recharge
nodes.x: A licensed Type-L stretched into a long-range coilgun for the Pavise. VEK fuel cells recharge it slowly, so it is used as a single-shot precision weapon. Funkenwerk's Aufbruch buffers it with a capacitor core and is the first frame to fire one on the run.

nodes.t: Coils wound in vacuum, a barrel cast in one piece
nodes.x: Shackleton Works' first weapon of its own. It started as the Type-L carbines Geneva fitted to the Tellus, and ended as something Mitsurugi can't make: coils wound in vacuum and a barrel cast in a single piece, firing faster and cooler than any coilgun on Earth. The Earthrise carries the carbine; the Defender carries the long rifle, and the Custodian a scaled-up one. The Republic gives them to the UN and sells them to nobody.

nodes.t: Building-sized point defence
nodes.x: Ground- and ship-based lasers that shoot down missiles. Building-sized, grid-powered, and far too weak to hurt armour.

nodes.t: Kills missiles, can't hurt armour
nodes.x: A shoulder laser that destroys incoming missiles, drawing from the Kestrel's linear-rifle packs. The first energy weapon in squadron service, and defensive only.

nodes.t: Five shots, then a 90-second cooldown
nodes.x: Tsukuyomi Lab's prototype particle beam rifle. Five shots that go through any armour, then ninety seconds to cool while it erodes its own barrel liner. It has never finished a trial without a fault, and every bloc wants it.

nodes.t: Cable-fed from a generator truck
nodes.x: OKB-7's brute-force answer: a particle cannon fed by cable from a generator truck. Immobile while firing, but nothing on the battlefield hits harder.

nodes.t: Vehicle and aircraft electronic warfare
nodes.x: Jamming pods, radar decoys and the datalinks that tie a battery to its radar. Every army had them before mechs. The Union took them most seriously.

nodes.t: Directive 5 in a shoulder pod
nodes.x: A broadband jammer and decoy emitter sized for a frame's shoulder, built for Directive 5: blind the enemy first, then fight. A lance switches them on together, so the enemy's sights, datalinks and missile seekers all go grey at once. The Pavise carries the heaviest set, and the Genette-E and Colibri-E carry the same pod on wheels and rotors.

nodes.t: Open-drawing jammer that shouts louder than everyone
nodes.x: Funkenwerk's answer to the Störer-5, which the Union wouldn't sell to a cooperative: a rig built from published drawings and civilian broadcast parts that drowns every frequency nearby in noise and music. It is cruder than the pod and three times as loud. Querschläger crews play their own records on it, and the Union's signals officers have learned most of the songs.

nodes.t: The network chooses the target, the battery fires
nodes.x: The datalink that lets Tianshu aim the Air Umbrella. Every Tiebi battery and Wanglou radar along the belt reports to the network, and the network decides which rack fires at which target, faster than any officer could. Crews still pull the trigger. They are told when.

nodes.t: One pilot, six uncrewed frames, one network
nodes.x: A Tianshu node built into a frame's torso, running the link to six uncrewed Tieshan conversions and the reactor under the pilot's seat. The network moves the squad and the pilot approves. Its weakness is the one Beijing doesn't discuss: jam the link and six frames stand still.

nodes.t: A battle-network mast that ties a hundred kilometres of lances together
nodes.x: Roland's horn: a command and sensor mast that pulls every lance within a hundred kilometres into one shared picture, and jams everything outside it. It is the Union's whole doctrine in one mast, and Castellani built it before the giant that carries it. In the song, Roland dies because he is too proud to sound his horn.

nodes.t: Orbital hull assembly
nodes.x: Pneumatic and explosive rivet drivers used to assemble station hulls.

nodes.t: Heavy industrial cutting
nodes.x: High-power plasma torches for cutting thick plate.

nodes.t: Magnetic cargo launcher
nodes.x: The magnetic track that throws cargo pods off the orbital elevators. The largest electromagnetic accelerator ever built.

nodes.t: Worker-frame tool, first used in anger
nodes.x: The standard hull-riveting tool on Ascension worker frames. It became a weapon during the first station labour dispute, when workers turned it on security frames.

nodes.t: Worker-frame hull cutter
nodes.x: The worker frame's hull cutter. Ascension sold the design to Castellani, which turned it into a sword.

nodes.t: Grapple and boarding line
nodes.x: A salvage tug's harpoon and winch. Militarised versions grapple and board, which is how most fights in orbit actually end.

nodes.t: Tungsten spikes, recoil-balanced
nodes.x: A militarised RD-9 firing tungsten spikes, with recoil balanced against the frame so the shooter doesn't go tumbling in zero gravity. Officially, it's still a construction tool.

nodes.t: Main gun of the first warships
nodes.x: A shortened section of elevator launch track fitted as the main gun of the first dedicated warships, built with Halcyon linear-rifle know-how under contract.

power.label: Power
power.intro: Every mech is short on power, and each bloc made a different trade. Brannock and Tianlong accepted noise and heat for endurance. Halcyon accepted forty minutes for silence. VEK accepted a hydrogen supply chain. Mitsurugi supplies the capacitors everyone else depends on. By 2186 Tianlong has accepted something stranger: reactors only its network is allowed to run.
turns: Brannock's turbine plumes showed on thermal sights kilometres away. Halcyon chose quiet, cool batteries and accepted forty minutes of endurance.
The swap pit became a battlefield
Ninety-second battery swaps made US ground crews a front-line arm, and made swap points a target.
VEK's quiet fuel cells needed depots, which became targets. The BZ-6 reformer fixed it by making hydrogen from ordinary diesel.
Fission (OKB-7), thorium salt run by a network (Tianlong), fusion (Mitsurugi) and beamed power (Halcyon and the Lunar Republic). Each one is a political crisis waiting to happen.
fams: Turbines and diesels. Loud, hot and dependable.
Silent and cool-running, but endurance is measured in minutes.
Quiet hydrogen power. The problem is the hydrogen.
Pulse power for linear and energy weapons. Almost all of it is Mitsurugi's.
Prototypes only. Unlimited endurance, unacceptable consequences.
Orbital power that could reach the ground.

nodes.t: Main battle tank engines
nodes.x: Multi-fuel gas turbines from main battle tanks. Compact and powerful, but they drink fuel and leave a hot exhaust plume.

nodes.t: Heavy commercial engines
nodes.x: Diesel engines from heavy trucks and locomotives. Heavy, low-tech, and repairable anywhere.

nodes.t: A tank turbine in a mech torso
nodes.x: Brannock-Hale's first frames ran on a modified tank turbine. Plenty of power and hours of fuel, but an exhaust plume thermal sights could see for kilometres.

nodes.t: Truck diesel driving a generator
nodes.x: A truck diesel turning a generator that feeds the limb motors. Heavy and loud, but any village mechanic can fix it. This is why Tianlong frames have such big torsos.

nodes.t: The Gruzovik's engine in a frame's back
nodes.x: The turboshaft from the K-26 Gruzovik helicopter, geared to a generator. It is light for its power, which an airborne frame needed, but it is thirsty, runs hot and screams. OKB-7 went back to diesels for everything after it.

nodes.t: Battery for sprints, turbine to cruise
nodes.x: A smaller turbine paired with a buffer battery. The mech sprints on battery, cruises on the turbine, and can shut the turbine down to cut its heat signature in an ambush. Brannock engineers won't admit the battery work came from Halcyon.

nodes.t: Burns diesel, kerosene, or worse
nodes.x: A tougher diesel that runs on almost any liquid fuel, including captured stocks and refinery waste. It's the main reason Pact armies need so little logistics. The Darkhan sheds pull them out of tractors for the Takhi and Bürged.

nodes.t: Two engines for heavy frames
nodes.x: OKB-7 heavy frames carry two Type-06-derived engines. One can fail and the frame still walks home. It powers the heavy arm actuators, onboard equipment and Grad-M ignition circuits.

nodes.t: Surplus GT-900s on local fuel
nodes.x: Surplus GT-900 turbines rebuilt to burn the League's own refinery output, with Type-06 fuel pumps grafted on. Hot and dirty, but the League makes all of its own fuel.

nodes.t: Mobile power for weapons too big for a mech
nodes.x: A wheeled generator built around four D-40 engines. It feeds the Iskra particle cannon by cable and recharges forward units. It's the first thing enemy pilots target.

nodes.t: Turbine charging an MHI capacitor bank
nodes.x: The frame-sized version of the plant Joint Heavy Systems first built at super-heavy scale for the Concord, and the power behind the AR-40E rifle. The turbine charges a licensed Mitsurugi capacitor bank, giving the Army pulse power without Halcyon's battery packs. Shrinking it to fit a 18 m frame is the hard part.

nodes.t: Electric vehicles, grid storage
nodes.x: Lithium-chemistry cells developed for electric vehicles and grid storage.

nodes.t: Fixed pack, forty minutes per charge
nodes.x: Halcyon's first frames used a fixed battery in the spine driving electric fans: quiet and cool-running, with no exhaust plume for thermal sights to find, but hours to recharge. Short endurance became part of US doctrine.

nodes.t: Hot-swapped in ninety seconds
nodes.x: A pack a ground crew can swap in ninety seconds with a frame-mounted crane. It made the swap pit a combat position and turned ground crews into a combat arm.

nodes.t: Battery plus capacitor, JSDF standard
nodes.x: Mitsurugi's design for Self-Defence Force frames: modest batteries with a large capacitor stage for bursts. Less endurance than Halcyon's packs, much better for energy weapons.

nodes.t: MHI capacitor buffer for the LR-3
nodes.x: Higher-density cells plus a Mitsurugi capacitor buffer that feeds the LR-3 rifle and PL-2 laser. The current Kestrel standard, and America's most export-restricted part.

nodes.t: Quiet hydrogen power
nodes.x: Hydrogen fuel cells from air-independent submarines and city buses.

nodes.t: Silent, but needs hydrogen depots
nodes.x: VEK's first frames used a fuel cell adapted from submarines. Near-silent and cold-running, but it needs hydrogen depots, and those became US strike targets.

nodes.t: Stackable modules that match hardpoints
nodes.x: Cells come in stackable modules, so a frame carrying heavy packs can carry extra power too. This is what makes the modular task group possible. Expensive, and very sensitive to contamination.

nodes.t: Makes its own hydrogen from diesel
nodes.x: Adds a reformer that strips hydrogen from ordinary diesel. Less efficient and slightly louder, but frames can now refuel from any truck, ending the depot problem. The Blitz pairs died for want of exactly this. Funkenwerk built the Querschläger around it, and the splinter carried the drawings to Darkhan, where the Tsagaan Salkhi burns herders' diesel in it.

nodes.t: Overdriven cells for aces
nodes.x: Castellani's hand-built stacks run at 140% of rated output. Spectacular performance, about two hundred hours before replacement, and only fitted to named aces' mechs.

nodes.t: Hydrogen split from station water
nodes.x: In orbit, hydrogen comes from water, which stations already recycle. Ascension's worker frames ran on fuel cells from the start.

nodes.t: Fuel cell with fold-out solar wings
nodes.x: Folding solar panels recharge the frame's electrolysers between shifts, so a worker frame can stay out for days. The militarised versions keep that endurance.

nodes.t: Polar ice, split by ring power and flown down sealed
nodes.x: Shackleton Works' first power plant for Earth, rebuilt from Ascension's station cell. The hydrogen comes from polar ice the Republic splits with ring power, and travels in sealed, swappable tanks flown down with every delivery, so a white squad never needs a hydrogen depot on Earth. The membranes are cast in vacuum, run cooler than anything VEK makes, and can't yet be made anywhere else.

nodes.t: For maglev and factory power
nodes.x: Before mechs, Mitsurugi built high-density capacitor banks for maglev lines and heavy industry. That product line turned out to be the key to every energy weapon since.

nodes.t: Backpack unit for the LR-1
nodes.x: The first mech-portable capacitor, sold to Halcyon for the LR-1 rifle. Large enough to need its own backpack.

nodes.t: The most licensed part in the world
nodes.x: Small enough to fit in a rifle stock. It's inside the LR-3, Type-L and PL-2, and is licensed or copied by every bloc. Japan's neutrality depends on it.

nodes.t: Mk.II built under licence
nodes.x: Licence-built Mk.II cores for the Spiegel coilgun and Castellani's projects. Mitsurugi deliberately sells VEK one generation behind.

nodes.t: Reverse-engineered Mk.I
nodes.x: Reverse-engineered from a captured Mk.I. It works, at twice the weight and half the charge life. Only elite Type-12 rail units get them.

nodes.t: Powers the BX-0, still overheats
nodes.x: Tsukuyomi Lab's prototype for the BX-0 beam rifle. It stores enough for five beam shots, and its discharge heat is why the rifle needs ninety seconds to cool.

nodes.t: Submarine and carrier plants
nodes.x: US pressurised-water reactors from submarines and carriers. Reliable at sea, enormous by mech standards.

nodes.t: Molten-salt fission from the Gansu desert
nodes.x: China's thorium programme, which began in the 2020s with a small test reactor in the Gansu desert that ran its fuel dissolved in molten salt. A salt reactor runs at ordinary pressure and needs no cooling water, so it can sit in a desert, and its fuel is a metal China has never been short of. The catch is control: the salt's chemistry has to be watched every minute it runs.

nodes.t: A thorium reactor on rails, run by the network
nodes.x: Tianlong's answer to a Fortress Belt that burns diesel faster than the railway can carry it: a salt reactor on four flatcars, parked behind the belt and feeding the dug-in Tiebis by cable while their diesels idle. Nobody on the train runs it. Tianshu watches the salt, the fuel and the load every second, decides which sector draws power the way it decides which train moves, and has the reactor cars shunted to a new siding before anyone has worked out where they were. The crews call it the stove. Beijing's engineers call it the first reactor no human operates.

nodes.t: A shielded mini-reactor in a heavy frame
nodes.x: OKB-7's secret test frame carries a shielded micro-reactor. Unlimited endurance on paper. In practice the pilot's radiation dose is measured, and every bloc fears what happens when one is shot down over a city.

nodes.t: A frame-sized salt reactor that only the network may run
nodes.x: The reactor train shrunk to fit inside a frame, which is only possible because no human has to run it. A Tianshu node rides with the core and holds the salt at temperature through every step, turn and recoil, trimming the load faster than a pilot could notice. If the frame falls, a plug of frozen salt melts and the fuel drains into a tank where it can't go critical. The pilot can't override any of it, by design. OKB-7's Pamir trusts a shielded pilot; Tianlong's core trusts nobody but the network. The Tianyan carries one in trials, and the Jingwei four.

nodes.t: Laboratory tokamaks
nodes.x: Decades of laboratory fusion work. Never net-positive outside a building-sized facility.

nodes.t: Too big for any normal frame; Japan's best-kept secret
nodes.x: Tsukuyomi Lab's compact fusion rig, using Mk.II capacitor tech for the ignition pulse. Far too big for a normal frame: the only mech that carries one is Takemikazuchi, built at 45 m to fit it. If it ever shrinks to fit an 18 m frame, the balance of power changes overnight.

nodes.t: Satellite and station power
nodes.x: Photovoltaic arrays powering satellites and early stations.

nodes.t: Powers the orbital elevators
nodes.x: Huge collectors around the elevator anchors that power the cargo launch tracks and stations. The largest power source in orbit, jointly owned by every bloc.

nodes.t: Beaming power to ground receivers
nodes.x: Ascension's experiment in beaming surplus ring power to ground receivers. Officially for disaster relief. Every military noticed it could recharge a mech.

nodes.t: Kestrels recharged by beam, never landing
nodes.x: Halcyon's classified program to recharge QX-3 packs from the ring's microwave relay mid-flight. Halcyon frames fly on electric fans, so beamed power keeps both the fans and the weapons running. If it works, America's forty-minute limit disappears, and there's a weapon-grade power beam over every battlefield. Test series ██-4 ended early. Cause of termination: ████████ ██ ███ ██████.

nodes.t: Beamed power, parked over a UN operation
nodes.x: The Republic's own answer to Ascension's relay test: relay satellites that take power from the ring and beam it down to a rectenna on a frame's back. The Republic has offered to park one over any UN operation, and under it a frame never runs dry. Halcyon is chasing the same idea for its fans and guns. The Republic gives it to the white squads for nothing.

doctrine.label: Doctrine
doctrine.intro: Each bloc's doctrine follows from its hardware and its constraints. The United States fights on a forty-minute battery clock, the Union blinds the enemy to make up for small numbers, and the Pact spends frames to save time. The rest improvise.
turns: Every bloc first used mechs to kill tanks, not other mechs. Mech-on-mech doctrine came later than anyone expected.
US drop-and-strike runs on battery endurance. The Union and Pact both built counter-doctrines around surviving the first forty minutes.
The Union's EW-led doctrine makes up for its small numbers. It's the main reason Continental lances punch above their weight.
Beijing's Tianshu network runs the walls and the Air Umbrella; Moscow runs the breakthrough groups and the augmented pilots. Pact doctrine is becoming two doctrines.
Nobody knows how to fight in orbit
Warships exist; space doctrine doesn't. The first real battle in orbit will rewrite every manual.
fams: Expeditionary forces. Speed, air power and a long Army–Air Force rivalry.
Small numbers, high quality. Blind the enemy, then fight.
Mass, firepower and acceptable losses. Beijing builds walls; Moscow builds breakthroughs.
Defensive by law, influential by industry, and running out of room.
Making do with everyone else's equipment.
Fighting where nobody has doctrine yet.
Borrowed frames from every bloc, and strict rules for when they may fire.

nodes.t: Armour holds, air power strikes deep
nodes.x: Pre-mech US doctrine: armour holds the front while air power strikes deep behind it.

nodes.t: Helicopter and tiltrotor assault
nodes.x: Infantry delivered by helicopter and tiltrotor behind or around the enemy front.

nodes.t: Mechs as mobile anti-tank guns
nodes.x: The Army's first mech doctrine. Pairs of Brannock frames with M30s and ATGM tubes ambushed tanks from terrain tanks couldn't cross, then fell back to friendly armour.

nodes.t: Frames slung under heavy-lift tiltrotors
nodes.x: Early Halcyon ground frames were carried under tiltrotors and dropped behind enemy lines. It worked, but the tiltrotors were easy kills, and that pushed Halcyon towards transformation.

nodes.t: Four-mech teams replace tanks in rough terrain
nodes.x: Four Brannock frames per team: two rifles, one Hornet pod, one M140 bazooka. Fire teams now replace tanks in mountains, forests and cities.

nodes.t: Fly in, land, fight, leave inside forty minutes
nodes.x: Kestrels fly in, strike with wing stores, land and fight with LR-3s, then transform and leave before their batteries run out. The forty-minute clock drives every plan; enemies call it “the forty-minute war”.

nodes.t: Army holds the ground, Air Force strikes
nodes.x: After years of rivalry, a joint mandate: Brannock fire teams seize and hold a swap point, and Kestrels strike from it. The services still argue over who commands.

nodes.t: Forward battery points as combat positions
nodes.x: Battery-swap pits within reach of the front. Ground crews are trained and armed as combat troops, and enemies now target pits before mechs.

nodes.t: Kestrels that never need to land
nodes.x: A draft doctrine written for the SKYLINE beamed-power program: Kestrels that stay airborne for hours. It doesn't work without SKYLINE, and nobody knows whether SKYLINE works.

nodes.t: Two ordinary soldiers, not one altered one
nodes.x: America's answer to the Volk and to the rumours about Koschei. Every US pilot serves unaltered, by regulation, and recruits are screened for implants. Halcyon and Brannock-Hale advertise their frames as built for ordinary people, and the Concord's two-pilot crew is presented as proof. In Washington, biological purity is starting to sound like patriotism.

nodes.t: Reconnaissance-in-force tradition
nodes.x: European armoured cavalry: fast reconnaissance units that find and fix the enemy for the main force.

nodes.t: Jamming and signals intelligence
nodes.x: Cold War electronic warfare: jamming, deception and signals intelligence.

nodes.t: Licensed frames scouting ahead of tanks
nodes.x: The first Union mechs, licensed Brannock frames, screened ahead of tank columns, using their height and sensors to see farther than vehicles could.

nodes.t: One frame, reconfigured per mission
nodes.x: The standard hardpoint means a lance of three VEK frames can be re-equipped for assault, defence or recon overnight. That's how the Union makes up for its small numbers.

nodes.t: Blind first, fight second
nodes.x: Every engagement opens with electronic attack: jam the sensors, spoof the data links, then attack while the enemy is blind. EW frames lead formations instead of following them.

nodes.t: EW frame, coilgun sniper, lance knight
nodes.x: Built to defeat drop-and-strike. An EW frame jams the Kestrels' landing approach, a Spiegel sniper shoots them as they transform, and a lance-armed frame finishes them on the ground.

nodes.t: Named aces in Castellani prototypes
nodes.x: The Union gives its best prototypes to famous aces and publicises their kills. Part morale, part propaganda, and part a way to sell member states on more spending.

nodes.t: Every program answers to a panel that can stop it
nodes.x: When the Union's parliament learned, from footage Geneva sent every member on the same morning, what Halden had sent into the Great Sand Sea in its name, it put every defence research program under an ethics panel with the power to halt it. Halden's Geneva laboratories are the panel's first case, and the hearings are still running. The Union is slower for it, and intends to stay that way.

nodes.t: Echeloned mass offensives
nodes.x: Offensives in successive echelons, each wave exploiting the gap the last one opened.

nodes.t: Fire as the decisive arm
nodes.x: Artillery as the arm that decides battles, used in enormous concentrations.

nodes.t: Six weeks of training, many frames
nodes.x: The Pact accepted early on that Tianlong frames were outclassed, and fields so many that the enemy runs out of ammunition first. Pilots train for six weeks.

nodes.t: Frames dropped behind the front
nodes.x: Deep battle from the air. Korsaks were dropped by parachute to seize passes and bridges ahead of the Tieniu waves, and to hold them until the column arrived. At Talysh the column never did. The order is still on the books, but no frame has been dropped under it since.
nodes.z: 2171 · the airborne divisions go back to light tanks

nodes.t: Ride ahead, carry everything, never wait
nodes.x: The doctrine the Takhi was first built for and the Tsagaan Salkhi perfected: a handful of fast frames that scout, strike and supply themselves, spread across a hundred kilometres of steppe and answerable to their own camp rather than a depot. Tianshu routes the trains. The wind riders decide where the trains will be needed. The idea goes up with the wind riders who leave for the Belt in the war, and becomes the Syndicate's rapid doctrine: speed, dispersal and self-supply, out where the plans arrive late.

nodes.t: Mechs as direct-fire artillery
nodes.x: Type-01 cannons could only fire braced, so mechs formed kneeling firing lines like artillery batteries. A technical workaround became the Pact's defining image.

nodes.t: Rockets, then cannons, then blades
nodes.x: Three waves: the first empties Grad-M batteries, the second kneels and fires Type-09s, the third closes with carbon blades. Each wave is timed to arrive as the one before runs dry.

nodes.t: Dug-in kneeling lines on the borders
nodes.x: Type-09 lines in prepared positions along the borders, mechs dug in to the shoulders. Very hard to dislodge, and the reason no bloc has invaded the Pact. Tianshu, which began by scheduling the belt's trains, now decides which sector the reserves go to.

nodes.t: OKB-7 heavies open the gap
nodes.x: OKB-7 heavy frames with demolition mauls and supporting cannons lead and punch a hole for the waves behind. The first change in Pact doctrine that values quality over numbers.

nodes.t: Engineered elites for the best frames
nodes.x: Conscript losses made elite pilots precious. The answer is Department Zero, a secret institute that augments pilots with implants and conditioning. Officially it doesn't exist. It is run from Moscow. Beijing's planners accept cybernetic links but refuse anything that rewrites the pilot, and say so at every staff meeting.

nodes.t: Massed AA rockets against Kestrels
nodes.x: Built to defeat drop-and-strike: Type-03 racks loaded with anti-air rockets fire massed volleys over fortress belts to deny landing zones. Cheap, crude and effective. Its batteries are cued by Tianshu, Beijing's planning network and the most automated command system any bloc has fielded.

nodes.t: Mongolian crews who scout ahead of the frame trains
nodes.x: Tianshu can route a frame train across Mongolia, but it can't see the pasture, the washed-out crossings or the herders who know both. Since the Fortress Belt went in, Mongolian and Kazakh crews have scouted the rail lines in stripped-down Tieniu, living in their frames for weeks between depots. They are austere, communal and the least predictable part of Tianshu's plans: they treat a frame like a horse, and don't leave a lame one behind. Beijing calls them the Steppe detachments.

nodes.t: Kalibr-305 and Iskra against cities
nodes.x: Draft doctrine for breaking fortified cities with siege mortars and cable-fed particle cannons. It assumes a long war, which is what worries the other blocs most.

nodes.t: The network proposes, the officer approves
nodes.x: Tianshu began as Tianlong's rail scheduler for the frame trains, grew into the planner behind the Fortress Belt, and learned to cue the Air Umbrella. Under Order 21 it drafts every operational plan from sensors, depot stocks and rail timetables, and officers approve or amend it. Officers who amend too often are retrained. Tianshu also grades them for reliability, and the criteria are listed only as ████████ ██ ███ ███████, ███████ ███████. Moscow's staff officers call it command by forecast.

nodes.t: Constitutional self-defence
nodes.x: A long-standing legal limit: Japanese forces exist only to defend Japan.

nodes.t: Trade as national strategy
nodes.x: Decades of national strategy built on high-value manufacturing exports.

nodes.t: Mechs first fielded for earthquakes
nodes.x: Japan's first mechs were rescue and recovery frames for earthquakes and tsunamis. The public trusted mechs before the military armed them.

nodes.t: Coasts and islands, with the navy
nodes.x: Self-Defence Force frames defend coastlines and outlying islands, deployed from amphibious ships with naval fire support. Type-L carbines and HC-2 hybrid cells.

nodes.t: Sell to everyone, depend on no one
nodes.x: Japan's real defence doctrine: license critical parts to every bloc so no one can afford to attack the supplier. It works as long as no bloc decides it would rather seize the factory.

nodes.t: JSDF units run MHI prototypes
nodes.x: Selected JSDF units take Mitsurugi prototypes into live exercises and the occasional real incident. The fastest test cycle in the world, and why so many prototypes end up in combat.

nodes.t: Armed pickups and militia
nodes.x: Irregular warfare built around armed pickup trucks and local militia.

nodes.t: Refusing bloc membership
nodes.x: A shared refusal to join any of the major blocs.

nodes.t: Surplus Gen 1 frames as militia fire support
nodes.x: The League's first mechs were surplus Gen 1 frames supporting militia, the mech equivalent of a gun on a pickup. They taught a generation of pilots to improvise.

nodes.t: Disperse, hide, strike, vanish
nodes.x: Small groups hide in dunes and sandstorms, strike convoys and depots, then scatter. The League rarely wins a pitched battle, so it avoids them.

nodes.t: No foreign bases, ever
nodes.x: League states deny bases to every bloc and keep enough mechs to make an incursion costly. The blocs fight proxy wars here instead.

nodes.t: Organised around interchangeable parts
nodes.x: League battalions mix frames from every bloc, organised around which parts interchange. Borrowed from the Continental modular idea, but driven by supply instead of choice.

nodes.t: People before territory
nodes.x: The Khartoum Charter's doctrine, written after the Jinn sightings. Frames are positioned to shield populations rather than to hold ground, and a battalion's first duty in any fight is evacuation. The Gulf associates call it soft. The Charter states point out that people still live in the Great Sand Sea.

nodes.t: Policing, not warfare
nodes.x: Security on early stations was policing: no heavy weapons, no military chain of command.

nodes.t: Ship-to-ship tradition
nodes.x: Centuries of ship-to-ship combat doctrine, none of it written for orbit.

nodes.t: Hired protection
nodes.x: Private firms hired to guard assets in unstable regions.

nodes.t: Armed worker frames after the labour dispute
nodes.x: After the first station labour dispute, Ascension crews formed armed militias with rivet drivers and torches. The consortium never fully disarmed them.

nodes.t: Harpoon, breach, seize
nodes.x: Most fights in orbit end with a harpoon and a cut hull, because nobody wants to destroy the station they're fighting over. Worker frames do it better than military ones.

nodes.t: Small elite teams, the best of every bloc
nodes.x: Grey Lantern Security fields small teams using the best frame from each bloc. It copied the US fire-team structure, then threw out the rules of engagement.

nodes.t: Fire only to protect
nodes.x: The white squads' first rules of engagement, written for the convoy escorts. A white frame fires only to protect a convoy, a camp or itself, never pursues, and never holds ground for anyone. Squads train to fight as mixed units whose frames share no parts, and their mechanics learn every bloc's wiring.

nodes.t: Protect, then pursue
nodes.x: Rewritten after Mong Hsat. When the Security Council names a threat to civilians, a white squad may go after it instead of waiting for it, and may finish it. Esteves calls it the narrowest possible exception. The squads who flew at Mong Hsat call it the Sawbwa rule.

nodes.t: First warships, no proven doctrine
nodes.x: The first dedicated warships carry mass drivers and mech catapults, but nobody has fought ship-to-ship in orbit. Every bloc is borrowing old naval thinking and hoping.

vehicles.label: Vehicles
vehicles.intro: Tanks, jets and helicopters didn't disappear when mechs arrived. They're cheaper, lower and harder to see than a 18 m frame, so every line adapted instead: roof armour and high-angle guns for tanks, escort and hunting roles for fighters, mast sights and fire-and-forget missiles for gunships. Later models borrow mech technology as it matures, from capacitor cores to point-defence lasers. The one role that did end is marked END. Drones are the cheapest of all, and every bloc now flies them in the thousands. Armies and companies without bespoke industry run on export and second-hand vehicles, built to sell to anyone.
turns: Garrisons ambushed a TL-80 column from a ravine tanks couldn't climb. Designers answered with roof armour, high-angle guns and hull-down tactics. A tank is 2.4 m tall and costs a quarter as much as a Teamster.
A mech can see over every ridge, but everyone can see a mech. Low vehicles became the ambushers: hull-down tanks, recon cars in hedgerows, and gunships just below the crest line.

A Kestrel is a ground frame that can fly, and a poor dogfighter. Fighters escort the drops, other fighters hunt them, and jets with hours of fuel fly the support missions a forty-minute battery can't.
Capacitor cores, electrothermal guns and point-defence lasers were built for frames, and they're now going into tanks, fighters and gunships. The BH-110 Regulator and the Kite IV are the result.

Beijing's Tiejia-V has no crew and a reactor no human runs. The Lunar Republic beams power to a truck. OKB-7 puts a particle cannon on tracks. The newest vehicles carry the frames' technology further than the frames do.
fams: Escorts, hunters, and jets that can stay longer than forty minutes.
Under the crest line, where a mech can't follow.
Small enough to lose. Jammers, raiders and the network's eyes.

nodes.t: America's main battle tank
nodes.x: Brannock-Hale's main battle tank: gas turbine, 125 mm gun, composite armour, and the fire-control system that later went into the Garrison. On open ground it was the best tank in the world.

nodes.t: Roof armour and a sensor mast after Iron Gate
nodes.x: Iron Gate showed what happens when the enemy fires from above. The A3 added roof armour against plunging fire, a sensor mast to see over ridges, and a gun that elevates far enough to hit a mech's torso. Crews learned to stay hull-down and let the frames give themselves away first.

nodes.t: The first tank designed to fight mechs
nodes.x: A low hull, heavy roof armour, a high-angle 125 mm gun, and a roof-mounted Hornet pod for shots at hip actuators. On open plains a Marshal II platoon costs about as much as one Teamster and spots a frame long before the frame finds it. Brannock fire teams own rough ground; Marshals own flat ground.

nodes.t: Point-defence laser borrowed from the Harrier
nodes.x: Hornet pods and Grad-M salvos made the roof the weak spot again. The A2 mounts a PL-2-derived laser on the turret to shoot down incoming missiles, fed from a capacitor buffer the turbine charges.

nodes.t: An electrothermal gun on a tank
nodes.x: A Marshal successor built around the HT-20 plant and an enlarged AR-40E electrothermal gun. It hits about as hard as a linear rifle, from a hull 2.4 m tall. The Army's mech lobby calls it a waste of capacitors. The tank lobby points out that it costs a quarter as much as a Pathfinder.

nodes.t: “Iron Armour”: cheap, low, exported by the thousand
nodes.x: Tianlong's mass-production tank: small, simple, and sold across Africa and Arabia. An insurgent column of them was the first armour ever destroyed by mechs, at Iron Gate. Thousands are still in service.

nodes.t: Taught to fight beside the Tieniu
nodes.x: After Iron Gate the Pact kept building tanks and taught them to work with mechs. Tiejia platoons guard the Tieniu's legs and flanks while the frames kneel to fire, and a raised gun mount lets them hit a frame's torso at close range. Cheap, plentiful and easy to crew.

nodes.t: Autoloader, reactive roof armour, export favourite
nodes.x: Built in the same factories as the Tieshan, on the same multi-fuel diesel. Reactive armour on the roof stops the plunging fire that kills older tanks, and the autoloader fires fast enough to hit a mech before it ducks back behind a ridge. The most exported tank in the world.

nodes.t: Fights in the gaps between kneeling Tieshans
nodes.x: Order 11 waves leave gaps between kneeling frames, and the TL-19 fills them. It's low and fast, with top-attack missiles in the turret and a Type-07 action as its coaxial gun. Every Tieshan company now has a Tiejia platoon assigned to protect its legs.

nodes.t: Turretless Tiejia hull, raid supply carrier
nodes.x: The League bought surplus TL-92s, cut off the turrets, and turned them into armoured carriers for fuel, ammunition and frame parts. The frames do the fighting, and the Kafila keeps them running between strikes. One convoy of them keeps the Jinn alive.

nodes.t: TL-99 hull with a refurbished shoulder cannon
nodes.x: The League's own tank: a surplus TL-99 hull carrying a Type-01Q cannon on mining-rig recoil dampers. It fires on the move, which no Tianlong vehicle ever managed with that gun, and it hides in dunes a Sirocco couldn't crouch behind.

nodes.t: Light enough for mountain bridges and landing ships
nodes.x: Japan's defensive tank, built light for mountain roads and amphibious ships. Mitsurugi's suspension work on it fed into the balance-control research behind every later MHI frame.

nodes.t: Wheeled, fast, shipped with the Hayates
nodes.x: Japan replaced the Type-78 with an eight-wheeled combat vehicle that rides the same landing ships as the Hayates. On island roads it outruns a frame, and its coil gun, derived from the Type-L, makes any intruder's mech think twice. The Hayates hold the beach; the Type-11s hold the roads behind it.

nodes.t: Air-droppable light tank
nodes.x: A light tank built to go under a tiltrotor with airborne infantry: thin armour and a 105 mm gun.

nodes.t: Re-roled as a mech ambusher
nodes.x: The Sparrowhawk took over the air-drop job, so the Army found the Ranger a new one. A low, fast tank with ATGMs in the turret can hide where a 18 m frame can't, and wait for a Tieniu to walk past. Ranger crews call it fighting from the ankles.

nodes.t: A purpose-built mech hunter
nodes.x: Two metres tall, quiet on hybrid drive, with a mast sight and top-attack missiles aimed at hip actuators. Hounds work in pairs ahead of a fire team, finding enemy frames and forcing them to stop and deal with something they can barely see.

nodes.t: The fire team's hidden fifth member
nodes.x: Data-linked to Teamster fire teams, so a Hound can fire Hornet cells at targets a Teamster has marked, and the other way round. Fire teams that train with a Hound pair lose fewer frames than teams that don't, which has quietly settled the argument about whether tanks still matter.

nodes.t: Wheeled recon with a telescoping sensor mast
nodes.x: The Union's reconnaissance car: fast, quiet, with a mast that raised its sensors eight metres.

nodes.t: Eyes that can't be seen
nodes.x: A mech sees farther from 17 m up, but it can be seen from everywhere. The Genette-B went passive: no radar, a low mast and thermal sights, so it could sit in a hedgerow and watch what the Écuyer screen could only guess at.

nodes.t: Ground jammer car
nodes.x: Directive 5 opens every fight with electronic attack, and the Genette-E delivers it from closer than any aircraft dares. It creeps to within a few kilometres of the enemy line, switches on, and moves before anyone can find it.

nodes.t: A decoy that looks like a lance
nodes.x: Built for the hunter-killer lance: a car that broadcasts the radar and radio signature of a Pavise. Enemy Kestrels see three lances where there's one, and the Genette-L doesn't mind being shot at, as long as it keeps moving.

nodes.t: Infantry fighting vehicle, 30 mm turret
nodes.x: America's infantry carrier: six dismounts in the back and a 30 mm chain gun on top. That chain gun, given a pistol grip, became the M30, the first mech weapon.

nodes.t: Up-armoured to keep up with mechs
nodes.x: Infantry still clear buildings and guard frames at rest. The A4 added armour and a frame-height periscope so its crew could follow a Garrison pair through ground the old Drover avoided.

nodes.t: Fire-team carrier with reload racks
nodes.x: One Drover II rides with each four-mech fire team, carrying dismounts, M140 reloads and spare stake-driver cylinders. It's the reason a Brannock team can fight for a day without falling back.

nodes.t: Armoured swap-pit carrier with a battery crane
