nodes.x: A Drover II hull with the M1100's flatbed: four QX-3 packs under armour, a fold-out crane, and a 30 mm turret for when the pit is attacked. Kestrels land beside it, swap in ninety seconds and leave. Pit crews call it the most shot-at vehicle in the Army.

nodes.t: A swap pit with no crew
nodes.x: Enemies target swap pits before they target mechs, so the Army is testing a Pitwagon with no crew. It drives to a grid reference, opens up, and swaps packs on its own. It works in trials. In its one live test, it was the first thing destroyed.

nodes.t: “Iron Thunder”: tracked 152 mm howitzer
nodes.x: The backbone of Pact massed artillery. Before mechs, batteries of these decided battles.

nodes.t: Indirect fire; shoot and move
nodes.x: Order 5's kneeling lines took over direct fire, but indirect fire still needed tubes. The TL-90 added an autoloader and shoot-and-move drills, because mech raids could now reach the gun lines.

nodes.t: Rocket artillery behind the fortress belt
nodes.x: Tracked rocket launchers alongside the tube guns: cheaper, quicker to move, and enough to break up an assault on a fortress belt before it reaches the kneeling lines.

nodes.t: “Watchtower”: radar and fire control for the Air Umbrella
nodes.x: A Leiting chassis with a folding radar and the fire-control link that makes Order 19 work. It cues hundreds of Tiebi rocket racks onto a Kestrel flight's landing approach at once. It's the only Pact vehicle with a higher protection priority than the mechs. Its fire-control link was the first time Tianshu aimed weapons rather than trains.

nodes.t: Tank transporter trucks and rail flats
nodes.x: Tanks wear out their tracks on long drives, so armies moved them by truck and rail. Mechs turned out to wear out their knees even faster.

nodes.t: Low-loader for a Garrison lying on its back
nodes.x: A Garrison walks at 30 km/h and needs new knee bearings every few hundred kilometres, so the US Army moves frames by road, lying flat on these. Every US frame since has had lift points for it.

nodes.t: Tracked, armoured carrier for a kneeling Tieshan
nodes.x: The M1100 idea on armoured TL-92 running gear. A Tieshan kneels on the back and rides to the line, saving its legs for the fight. Pact frame companies arrive by carrier, step off the back, and are firing within a minute.

nodes.t: Follows Koschei on tracks, feeding it by cable
nodes.x: Frame-carrier running gear scaled up until it can carry a micro-reactor and an MTU-7 generator stack. It follows Koschei on its own tracks. The cable between them is the one part Department Zero can't armour.

nodes.t: An ice-road hauler that carries a frame
nodes.x: Boreal built ice-road haulers before it built frames, so its first frame carrier was a hauler: a tracked over-snow tractor with a heated deck for a Tundra lying down, and a cab that can keep two drivers alive if the road gives way. Norway bought them before Ottawa did.

nodes.t: A scout car that runs as cold as the snow
nodes.x: The Wolverine's companion: a low, insulated scout car that lies up for days on a reformer-stack trickle with nothing switched on but its passive sensors. It finds the enemy, and the Wolverines decide what to do about it. Its customers are increasingly Union.

nodes.t: An open-drawing scout car from Tempelhof
nodes.x: Funkenwerk's second product and its first sold in numbers: a light scout car on a modular cell stack, built to keep up with a Läufer screen and fixable with whatever fits. The drawings are public, so the Dutch contingent built forty of its own and Funkenwerk printed that on a poster too.

nodes.t: “Foal”: the supply mule that follows the wind riders
nodes.x: A tracked mule from the Darkhan sheds that follows a Bürged across the steppe carrying fuel, ammunition and a felt tent. It runs on a tractor's multi-fuel diesel, steers itself between waypoints, and can be fixed by any herder's mechanic. The wind riders say the Unaga is why they never wait for a depot.

nodes.t: Ex-mining trucks, painted white
nodes.x: The UN has no vehicle maker, so the white convoys ran on whatever members gave: ex-mining haul trucks with welded-on armour, surplus Drovers and Kafilas bought second-hand, all stripped of markings and painted white. Efua Mensah wrote the drill: a white convoy stops for any convoy that asks, whoever owns it.

nodes.t: Beamed power, delivered by truck
nodes.x: Shackleton Works' ground station for the Relay Rectenna: a tracked mast that catches the Republic's beam and passes it to the white squads' frames within a few kilometres. It travels with UN operations, and the Republic parks a relay satellite over it for as long as Geneva asks. Under it, an Earthrise never runs dry.

nodes.t: An ace's transporter and racing pit
nodes.x: Castellani delivers each frame the way an Italian team delivers a racing car: in a red-and-gold transporter with a workshop inside, a crane, spare Stack-R cells and the engineers who tuned them. A Falco never fights far from its Bisarca, which is how the Union's enemies find it.

nodes.t: A chariot for a sworn pair
nodes.x: Nashik's carrier for an Ashvin pair: two frame cradles side by side, a shared cab for both pilots on the road, and the unit store where their augmentation rigs are kept between sorties, logged in and logged out under the Oath. Built on licensed TL-12 running gear, cooled for the plains.

nodes.t: A particle cannon on tracks, cable and all
nodes.x: The Iskra can't move while it fires, so OKB-7 gave it a carriage: a tracked mount for the cannon, coupled by cable to an MTU-7 generator truck a few hundred metres back. The pair is slow, loud and visible from orbit, and nothing on the battlefield hits harder.

nodes.t: A coilgun battery on a coastal truck
nodes.x: Japan's coastal defence moved its newest capacitor onto wheels: a Type-11 chassis carrying a Mk.III core and a long coilgun, able to fire from a beach and leave before anything answers. Beijing's customs seizures began a month after its first trials.

nodes.t: A tank with no crew and a reactor no human runs
nodes.x: Beijing's first uncrewed tank: a Tiejia-IV hull with a Salt Core, a Drum Rifle and no hatches at all. Tianshu drives it, aims it and runs its reactor, and a Tianyan pilot approves what it does. Six walk beside each trial squad. Moscow calls it a train with a gun.

nodes.t: “Crescent”: an armoured ambulance and water carrier
nodes.x: Protect First on tracks: a Kafila hull rebuilt as an armoured ambulance, with a water plant, a surgical bay and room for twelve stretchers. It follows the Harmattans into towns they have come to shelter. The Gulf associates asked what it was armed with, and Khartoum said water.

nodes.t: The Union's main battle tank
nodes.x: A fast, autoloaded tank built for the cavalry tradition: lighter than a Marshal, quicker across country, and fitted with the best fire control in Europe.

nodes.t: A sensor mast and a place behind the screen
nodes.x: After the Maghreb Depot Strikes the Union stopped sending tanks in first. The Hussard-B waits hull-down behind the Écuyer screen, its mast up, and fires at whatever the screen finds.

nodes.t: A tank that jams before it shoots
nodes.x: The first Union tank built for Directive 5: a Störer pod on the turret, Fenrir missiles in the bustle, and a quiet fuel-cell drive for the last kilometre. Its crews call the main gun the second weapon.

nodes.t: A coilgun on tracks, buffered by a licensed core
nodes.x: A Cuirassier rebuilt around the Spiegel coilgun, with a Licensed Core to recharge it faster than the Pavise can. It fights beside the hunter-killer lances and kills what they blind. Funkenwerk calls it the Union buying its own idea back.

nodes.t: The ethics panel's first tank
nodes.x: A prototype the ethics panel had to approve line by line: a coilgun, a jammer mast and a crew of two who can override every automated system aboard. It is slower to fight than anything Beijing builds, on purpose. Strasbourg calls it accountable. Its crews call it the committee.

nodes.t: “Knight”: Russia's heavy tank
nodes.x: A heavy, low tank with a 152 mm gun and an autoloader, built to break through prepared defences in the deep-battle tradition. It is slower than a Marshal and harder to stop.

nodes.t: Roof armour and rockets for the Caspian
nodes.x: The Vityaz after Talysh, where Merlins killed tanks from above: reactive roof armour, a Type-03 rocket rack for walking targets, and orders to stay close to the Tieniu.

nodes.t: “Ram”: the second wave's tank
nodes.x: Built to arrive with the second wave of an echeloned assault, when the Grad-M batteries have emptied and the defenders are reloading. Twin diesels, a 152 mm gun and a dozer blade for the craters the first wave left.

nodes.t: The Molot on tracks, ahead of the Mamonts
nodes.x: The breakthrough groups' tank: a Molot autoloading cannon in a turret, the same OKB-7 autoloader used by other heavy frames. It goes into the gap first and the Mamonts widen it. At the Hari River, more Taran-2s were lost than Mamonts, which is the point.

nodes.t: A siege tank for the Krepost's escort
nodes.x: Moscow's tank for a long war: a Taran-2 hull with city-breaking armour, a Molot and a mine plough, built to walk beside the Krepost and the siege trains into fortified towns. Every bloc's analysts have noticed where the plough is aimed.

nodes.t: A truck, a gun and a crew who know the ground
nodes.x: The vehicle of every irregular war before mechs: a commercial pickup with a machine gun or recoilless rifle bolted to the bed. Cheap, fast and everywhere.

nodes.t: A pickup that can kill a frame
nodes.x: The Convoy Raids' great equaliser: a desert pickup carrying a bootleg Hornet pod or a pair of salvaged ATGM tubes, hidden under a tarpaulin until a frame walks past. Nobody builds them and everybody sells them. Qadira's crews learned their trade on them, and so did half of Grey Lantern's.

nodes.t: A mine-proof truck sold to anyone
nodes.x: A V-hulled armoured truck built under licence in a dozen countries and sold to all of them: mine-resistant, easy to fix and big enough for a squad or a load of frame parts. The League rode in them, the white convoys painted them, and Grey Lantern buys them by the shipload under whatever flag it is using that year.

nodes.t: Same truck, now with a pod and a jammer
nodes.x: The Kopje after twenty years of frame wars: a Hornet-pattern pod on a ring mount, a cheap jammer copied from the Störer, and a winch for dragging a downed frame out of a fire zone. It is the most common armoured vehicle in Africa.

nodes.t: A recovery truck that can lift a frame
nodes.x: A six-wheeled crane truck with a winch, a frame cradle and a workshop in the back, built in Turkey, Brazil and South Africa from whichever parts were cheapest that year. Nobody's doctrine mentions it and every army without a Pitwagon runs on it.

nodes.t: A recovery truck that can also refuel a frame
nodes.x: The Mule with a Q-Mix generator and a battery bank, so it can recharge a hybrid frame or a Kopje as well as lift one. The Charter's armies take them everywhere, and Grey Lantern rents them by the week.

nodes.t: Loitering munitions and spotter drones
nodes.x: The drone war that came before mechs: cheap quadcopters, loitering munitions and long-range spotters, fought over by jammers on both sides. Mechs didn't end it. They gave it bigger targets.

nodes.t: “Dragonfly”: a jammer you can throw away
nodes.x: Directive 5's cheapest weapon: a small jammer drone that a Haubert lance launches by the dozen before contact. Each one screams on a different band until it is shot down, and every one shot down is a shot not fired at a frame.

nodes.t: Desert drones built from hobby parts
nodes.x: The raid bands' eyes in the Convoy Raids: hobby airframes with phone cameras and a grenade under the wing, launched from a pickup and flown off a laptop. They found convoys for Abu Ghubar a day before the convoys found him, and taught every bloc to watch the sky over the dunes.

nodes.t: The network's eyes along the belt
nodes.x: Thousands of small spotter drones that circle the Fortress Belt and report everything they see to Tianshu, which decides what matters. They cue the Air Umbrella's racks and the Wanglou radars. Nobody flies them; the network does.

nodes.t: Drones that keep the link alive
nodes.x: Beijing's quiet answer to the question nobody asks about the Tianyan: what happens when the link is jammed. A ring of relay drones flies above each squad, re-routing the link around any jammer they find. In trials the Union's Libelles grounded half of them in a minute.

nodes.t: A drone that waits, then dives
nodes.x: Mass-produced loitering munitions sold in crates of twenty, each one circling until it finds a hot engine or a frame's knee and diving on it. They are the cheapest anti-frame weapon ever built, and every bloc's jammers exist partly because of them.

nodes.t: Halcyon's strike fighter
nodes.x: The fighter whose wing binders, avionics and flight-control software every Halcyon frame inherited. It ruled the air in the decade before mechs.

nodes.t: Escort for the first variable frames
nodes.x: Built on the same line as the Merlin. The Merlin could fly but couldn't dogfight, so Gyrfalcon IIs escorted every Merlin flight and dealt with interceptors while the frames transformed and landed. Escorting frames became the American fighter's main job.

nodes.t: Escort for drop-and-strike
nodes.x: Designed around a Kestrel's two worst moments: landing and take-off. Lanners hold the air over a landing zone for forty minutes, then cover the climb-out. In the Forty-Minute War they kept Kestrel losses low, until the Pact's advisers switched to hitting the swap pits.

nodes.t: Laser defence on a capacitor bank
nodes.x: After the Sapsan, escort fighters had to survive rocket salvos too. The Saker carries a PL-2-derived laser and a Mitsurugi capacitor buffer charged by its engines, the first fighter to run on mech power technology. Saker pilots train alongside the Harriers they escort.

nodes.t: Armoured ground-attack jet
nodes.x: A slow, armoured jet built around a rotary cannon for killing tanks, with hours of loiter time.

nodes.t: Learned to hunt walking targets
nodes.x: A mech is the tallest thing on the battlefield and can't hide in a fold of ground. Shrikes were rearmed with heavier cannon rounds and top-attack bombs aimed at hip and knee actuators, and flew low enough to stay under early mechs' sensors.

nodes.t: Hours of support a Kestrel can't give
nodes.x: Kestrels raid; Shrikes stay. With hours of fuel against a Kestrel's forty minutes, the Shrike II flies the long support missions, firing glide munitions from beyond Hornet range. The Army asks for Shrikes by name, which the Air Force pretends not to notice.

nodes.t: “Swift”: OKB-7's high-speed interceptor
nodes.x: Before it built mechs, Kirov-Mikoyan OKB-7 was a fighter bureau. The Strizh was built to catch US bombers, and the bureau's heavy, aggressive engineering carried straight into the Medved.

nodes.t: Look-down radar for walking targets
nodes.x: Re-radared to find mechs moving through broken ground. At the Talysh Mountains it found the Merlins too late: they had already transformed and gone.

nodes.t: “Peregrine”: built to catch Kestrels mid-transformation
nodes.x: Designed after the Forty-Minute War around one number: the two seconds a Kestrel spends half-folded, too slow to fly and too high to fight. Sapsans circle over landing zones and dive into that window with short-range missiles. With the Air Umbrella, they're why the Harrier carries a point-defence laser.

nodes.t: Rocket salvos too big for one laser
nodes.x: OKB-7's answer to the Harrier: rocket salvos too large for one PL-2 to stop, and a dive that clears the landing zone before the Harriers' wingmen can reply.

nodes.t: “Swallow”: the Union's multirole fighter
nodes.x: A good, expensive European fighter, bought in small numbers by every Union member.

nodes.t: Lost the Maghreb air battle, changed jobs
nodes.x: In the Maghreb Depot Strikes, US pilots out-flew the Hirondelles and destroyed the Union's hydrogen depots in two weeks. The Union stopped trying to beat the Americans fighter for fighter, and rebuilt the Hirondelle around jamming instead of dogfighting.

nodes.t: The fast end of Directive 5
nodes.x: A two-seat electronic-attack fighter, with jammers in place of half its missiles and a back-seater who blinds enemy radar before the Haubert lances move. It scores fewer kills than the old Hirondelle and has far more influence on the fight.

nodes.t: Interceptor for the hunter-killer lance
nodes.x: The air half of Directive 8. Martinets wait over a Kestrel flight's predicted landing zone, cued by Pavise jammers on the ground, and attack the Kestrels on approach. The Spiegels take the ones that make it down.

nodes.t: “Swan”: swing-wing strategic bomber
nodes.x: OKB-7's intercontinental cruise-missile carrier.

nodes.t: Standoff missiles for swap pits and carriers
nodes.x: The Forty-Minute War showed the Pact where the United States is weakest: the swap pits and the carriers that feed its Kestrels. The Lebed-M fires long-range missiles at both from far outside US fighter cover.

nodes.t: Airborne radar and jamming aircraft
nodes.x: A converted airliner with a rotating radar dome and jamming pods: the eyes of Union air defence.

nodes.t: Rebuilt as a flying jammer after Maghreb
nodes.x: After the Maghreb strikes the Argus fleet was rebuilt for electronic attack, with fewer radars and far more jammers. It flew the first Directive 5 engagements, blinding enemy sensors before the Écuyers moved.

nodes.t: Command jammer for VEK lances
nodes.x: Data links to every Haubert lance and enough jamming power to blind a division. It was also the biggest, slowest target over any battlefield, and the Air Umbrella proved it.

nodes.t: Pulled back, still in charge
nodes.x: Once Pavises could jam from the ground, the Argus moved to high altitude far behind the line. It no longer jams the enemy. It ties every lance, Pavise and Martinet into one picture, which is a harder job to replace.

nodes.t: Strategic jet airlifter
nodes.x: Halcyon's four-engine transport, built to carry tanks to wars across an ocean.

nodes.t: One Garrison, lying down
nodes.x: A strengthened floor and a longer ramp let it carry one Garrison or Sparrowhawk across an ocean. America's whole expeditionary model depended on them.

nodes.t: Frame airlifter: three Kestrels or two Teamsters
nodes.x: The first airlifter designed around mechs, with a nose and tail that both open so frames can walk straight through. Rough-strip landing gear lets it land close enough to the front to matter. It exists because the Heron Heavy proved that frames slung under rotors get shot down.

nodes.t: A swap pit that flies in
nodes.x: A Condor that lands on a road, lowers both ramps and becomes a swap pit, with forty QX-3 packs, two cranes and an Osprey aboard. It's gone again within the hour. Sapsan pilots hunt Condor Pits as hard as they hunt Kestrels.

nodes.t: Re-beams orbital power to Kestrels under the clouds
nodes.x: A Condor airframe with a rectenna on top and a transmitter underneath. It catches power from the ring's microwave relay above the weather and passes it down to SKYLINE Harriers. If it works, the forty-minute clock lasts as long as the relay stays up.

nodes.t: A fighter that never has to land to recharge
nodes.x: The Saker rebuilt around SKYLINE: a rectenna in the spine draws beamed power from the relay above the clouds, feeding a Mk.III-buffered laser that can now hurt more than missiles. Under the relay it escorts Kestrels for as long as the beam holds. Away from it, it is a very expensive Saker.

nodes.t: An electrothermal gun with wings
nodes.x: The Shrike line's answer to frames that shrug off 30 mm: the Regulator's electrothermal gun along the belly and armour that takes a Drum Rifle burst. It loiters for hours over a fire team, which is the one thing a Kestrel still can't do.

nodes.t: “Golden Eagle”: a rail gun in the spine
nodes.x: Moscow's heavy interceptor, built after Harriers learned to laugh at rocket salvos: a Type-12 rail gun along the spine, fed by a Copied Core, to kill a Harrier beyond the reach of its laser. It needs a long runway and a longer budget. Beijing was not offered one.

nodes.t: “Kite”: the lance's own fighter
nodes.x: The Martinet grown into an electronic-warfare fighter that flies with a Pavise lance rather than above it: a Störer pod under each wing, two dozen Libelles in the bay, and Fenrir missiles for anything that switches on a jammer of its own. The ethics panel insisted on a pilot. The pilots insisted on two.

nodes.t: An uncrewed strike jet flown by the network
nodes.x: Beijing's first combat aircraft in a generation, because it waited until it didn't need pilots. Tianshu flies the Kunpeng in flocks of twelve, cueing strikes from the Spotters' picture and handing targets to the Air Umbrella. It has no cockpit, so it turns harder than anything with a person inside. It is named for the fish of the old story that became a bird so large its wings hid the sky.

nodes.t: A turboprop attack plane any air force can afford
nodes.x: A light turboprop that flies off dirt strips with guns and rockets under the wings, sold to every air force without a fighter budget. It can't survive a Sapsan. It never meets one.

nodes.t: A turboprop that hunts frames
nodes.x: The Hornbill with a mast sight, a Hornet pod and armour around the engine. League squadrons fly them, Grey Lantern leases them with pilots, and the white squads borrowed two for Mong Hsat.

nodes.t: Old airliners that carry one frame, lying down
nodes.x: Retired wide-body airliners with the floor reinforced and the nose cut to open, bought second-hand and flown by crews who don't ask what's in the hold. Each carries one frame on its back. Grey Lantern's airline has never had the same name twice.

nodes.t: Tank-hunting attack helicopter
nodes.x: Halcyon's attack helicopter. It hid behind ridges, popped up to fire missiles, and dropped back down.

nodes.t: A mast sight above the ridge, the rest below it
nodes.x: A mech's sensor head sees over the ridges Kites used to hide behind. The HH-52's answer was a mast-mounted sight, so only a ball the size of a football shows above the crest while the airframe stays hidden. After that, Kites found Tieniu more often than Tieniu found Kites.

nodes.t: Fire-and-forget missiles aimed at the knees
nodes.x: Kite IIIs escort Brannock fire teams and hunt enemy frames from behind, aiming at knee and hip actuators to leave a frame stranded rather than destroyed. Hornet anti-air pods keep them low and careful, but they're still the fastest anti-mech weapon a commander can call in.

nodes.t: Quiet hybrid drive and a point-defence laser
nodes.x: The first gunship built with mech technology: an HT-12-style hybrid drive that lets it hover on batteries with the turbines throttled back, and a small PL-2-derived laser to shoot down anti-air rockets. It's the only rotorcraft with a chance under the Air Umbrella.

nodes.t: Tiltrotor assault transport
nodes.x: Halcyon's tiltrotor, carrying airborne infantry with a Ranger light tank slung underneath.

nodes.t: Flew the Sparrowhawk drops
nodes.x: A heavy-lift Heron built to sling a stripped-down Sparrowhawk. In the Tiltrotor Drops at the end of Iron Gate the frames did well and the Herons did not: nine were shot down in a month. Halcyon's answer was a mech that could fly itself in. The airframe stayed in service; the role didn't.
nodes.z: 2166 · frame drops end; the Merlin flies itself in

nodes.t: Flies battery packs to the swap pits
nodes.x: Herons stopped carrying frames and started carrying what frames need. A Pit Runner slings four QX packs or a load of LR-3 magazines to a forward swap pit, and leaves before anyone starts shooting at the pit.

nodes.t: “Truck”: the world's biggest helicopter
nodes.x: Big enough to lift a light tank. A 72-tonne Tieniu was another matter.

nodes.t: Spare limbs and shell reloads
nodes.x: It can't lift a frame, so it lifts everything else: replacement legs, Type-01 shells and rocket racks, flown straight to kneeling lines the trucks can't reach.

nodes.t: Grad-M reloads within the hour
nodes.x: Bigger rotors and an underslung cradle for Grad-M batteries, so a wave's first salvo can be reloaded within the hour. Pact crews call it the second salvo.

nodes.t: Light scout helicopter
nodes.x: A small, quiet scout helicopter that spotted for Union armoured cavalry.

nodes.t: Spotter for the Écuyer screen
nodes.x: The Colibri flies below the treeline behind the Écuyers and lifts a mast sight over the trees to look where they're looking. It's smaller and quieter than any frame, and it sees what a mech's own height gives away.

nodes.t: Light jammer helicopter
nodes.x: A Colibri with a jamming pod, flying low over a Union lance to extend its electronic attack. It's cheap enough to lose, which is the point.

nodes.t: “Bumblebee”: armoured assault helicopter
nodes.x: OKB-7's heavy assault helicopter: armoured, rocket-armed, and able to carry a squad in the back.

nodes.t: “Orca”: gunship for the mech waves
nodes.x: OKB-7's answer to the Kite: a heavily armoured gunship that flies just behind Order 11 waves, firing rockets into whatever the kneeling lines flush out. It trusts its armour more than its sights, which suits Pact crews.

nodes.t: Flies inside the Air Umbrella
nodes.x: Built to fly under the Pact's own rocket umbrella, with identification gear the Wanglou trusts. It hunts Kestrels in the few seconds after they land, when they're down but not yet ready to fight.

nodes.t: A gunship with two uncrewed wingmen
nodes.x: The Kite IV with a second job: it flies with two uncrewed Kites that carry the missiles while the crewed one stays below the ridge. Washington says a person always pulls the trigger. Under Unaltered Crews, it is careful to say which person.

nodes.t: A utility helicopter for everyone
nodes.x: A medium twin-engine helicopter built for oil rigs, forestry and mining, and bought by every army that couldn't afford a Heron. It carries a squad, a load of frame parts slung underneath, or a casualty out of somewhere bad.

nodes.t: Door guns and a rocket pod
nodes.x: The Ibis with armour on the floor, door guns and a rocket pod on each side. It isn't a gunship, but it is the gunship most of the world's armies have. The keepers fly one, painted white, to carry the Jinn's patients to Khartoum.

carriers.label: Carriers
carriers.intro: How mechs get to the fight. Carriers began as converted amphibious ships, armoured trains, mining crawlers and cargo airships, and each bloc's carriers follow its geography. This tree runs past the present into the war years, where the first warships built to fight in the atmosphere appear, and ends where the carriers of No Peace Past Luna begin. Dashed cards in the war columns are projected; they haven't happened yet.
turns: A reactor is a battery charger
Merlins proved variable frames could land on a carrier deck. The Navy noticed that one carrier reactor could recharge a whole squadron's batteries at once.
Every bloc carries frames its own way
The United States goes by sea, the Pact by rail and ground-effect craft, and the League by mining crawler and old car ferry.
America's only helicarrier stays up nine hours on turbines. It's a carrier, not a warship, and it is never taken near a fight.
In orbit, carriers learn that frames win boarding actions but are too slow for open space, so they launch fighter craft beside them. Every carrier in 2327 still does.

Fusion and fission make lift cheap enough to armour. The Aerie and the Tsitadel are the first ships built to fight in the air instead of just carrying frames to it, and the last: the Lunar Mandate bans them.
fams: Flight decks that became swap pits.
From cargo airships to the first warships of the sky.
Tenders, catapult ships, and the way down.

nodes.t: Catapults, arresting wires and ninety jets
nodes.x: America's fleet carriers: nuclear-powered, catapult-launched, and built around Halcyon's Gyrfalcons. Their reactors turned out to matter more than their flight decks.

nodes.t: Variable frames on a carrier deck
nodes.x: Halcyon landed Merlins on a supercarrier to prove they could operate at sea. The real finding was below deck: one carrier reactor could recharge every battery spine in a squadron at once, where a shore base needed hours.

nodes.t: Supercarrier rebuilt as a floating swap pit
nodes.x: Kestrels don't need catapults; they need batteries. The United States rebuilt its supercarriers with swap bays where the catapults had been, charged straight off the reactor. One carrier can turn around forty Kestrels an hour without a single swap pit ashore.

nodes.t: Reactor-fed point-defence lasers
nodes.x: After Svalbard the Kestrel carriers were refitted for Harriers and given point-defence lasers fed directly from the reactor, so they can fire for as long as the ship has steam. It's the best-defended swap pit in the world.

nodes.t: Beams reactor power to Harriers overhead
nodes.x: A Harrier carrier with a SKYLINE transmitter on its island, beaming reactor power to any Harrier in line of sight. It does what the ring's relay does, without needing the Republic's permission. The Navy's carriers end up in orbit, but they keep the shape: the Ironshield of 2327 still has a supercarrier's flat deck and point defence fed straight off the reactor, and American doctrine still calls carriers flying citadels.

nodes.t: Well decks, tiltrotors and landing craft
nodes.x: Big-deck amphibious ships carrying marines, tiltrotors and landing craft, with a floodable well deck in the stern.

nodes.t: Garrisons standing in the well deck
nodes.x: Amphibious ships with raised hangars and a rebuilt well deck so Garrisons could stand upright. A Garrison can't swim, so landing craft carried them ashore two at a time. Six frames per ship, and the crew slept in what had been the vehicle deck.

nodes.t: The first ship designed around mechs
nodes.x: Tall hangars, frame-sized lifts, and a well deck Teamsters can wade out of in four metres of water. It lands a full fire-team company with its Drover IIs, then stays offshore as their workshop.

nodes.t: Flat-deck ships Japan won't call carriers
nodes.x: Flat-deck “destroyers” that are carriers in all but name, kept small and defensive by law.

nodes.t: Rescue frames delivered by sea
nodes.x: A helicopter destroyer refitted to carry Kizuna rescue frames to earthquake and tsunami zones. The Japanese public watched mechs walk off a ship on live television and start digging people out of rubble.

nodes.t: Island defence from the sea
nodes.x: A fast landing ship for Japan's outlying islands, with a stern ramp and a frame deck. It put the Hayates into the surf at Yonaguni during the Yaeyama Incidents.

nodes.t: Union amphibious ships for the Mediterranean
nodes.x: Union member navies' helicopter carriers and dock ships, built for evacuations and peacekeeping around the Mediterranean.

nodes.t: Fast ship for a modular task group
nodes.x: A fast roll-on, roll-off hull carrying three lances and every hardpoint module they might need. Crews refit the frames during the crossing, so the task group arrives already set up for its mission. Union carriers still work this way in 2327: the Luftkogge runs a multinational task group from its bridge, and the Martian Research Directorate's Vanguard refits its fighters between missions.

nodes.t: Icebreaker hull for the Arctic lances
nodes.x: Built for the Arctic seabed dispute: an icebreaker hull, heated hangars, and a reformer plant that refuels BZ-6 stacks from the ship's own diesel. It carried the lance that fought at Svalbard.

nodes.t: A Polar Carrier frozen in for the refugees
nodes.x: Projected. When the Canadian Front breaks, one Polar Carrier's Canadian crew take refugees north instead of home, and let the ice close around the hull in a fjord on Ellesmere Island. The reformer plant and heated hangars built to keep a lance warm keep a town alive through the winters, on whatever diesel they can find. The survivors call the ship the Hearth. When their descendants go out into the dark, they name their carriers after it.
nodes.z: Frozen in · its people carry the name into the dark

nodes.t: Bow-ramp ships for the Caspian and Pacific coasts
nodes.x: Pact landing ships: bow ramps, short range, built in numbers.

nodes.t: Tieniu over the beach in Azerbaijan
nodes.x: Landing ships with reinforced decks for kneeling Tieniu, used to put frames on the Caspian coast during the crisis. A Tieniu lying on a ramp can't fire back, and Merlins took advantage.
nodes.z: 2174 · the Pact moves frames by rail and ground-effect instead

nodes.t: Commercial vehicle shipping
nodes.x: Civilian roll-on, roll-off ferries and container ships. Every navy quietly counted them as reserve sealift.

nodes.t: Old car ferries with frames on the car decks
nodes.x: League states bought retired vehicle ferries and carry frames along the Red Sea and Gulf coasts in them, lying down on the car decks. Cheap, deniable and unarmoured.

nodes.t: A container ship that is secretly a mech base
nodes.x: Grey Lantern's floating base looks like any container ship in any port. Some of its containers are workshops, some are hangars, and two open into a launch rail for Lantern Customs. It's registered under a different flag every year.

nodes.t: Rail-mounted guns and troops
nodes.x: A Eurasian tradition that never died: armoured trains guarding borders across distances no road network covers.

nodes.t: Kneeling Tieniu on armoured flatcars
nodes.x: Tieniu walk slowly and break down often, so the Pact moved them by rail. Kneeling on braced flatcars, they could fire their shoulder cannons straight off the train. Their timetables came from a Tianlong logistics program called Tianshu, the first time the Pact let software decide where its frames went.

nodes.t: Trains that feed the fortress belt
nodes.x: A railway running behind the fortress belt that carries Tieshans, Tiebis and ammunition to whichever sector is under attack. The belt works because the trains move reserves faster than an enemy can walk. Tianshu writes the timetables, and reroutes them faster than any staff officer could.

nodes.t: The flatcars under the tarpaulins
nodes.x: Wide-gauge trains bringing Kalibr-305s, Iskras, MTU-7s and Tsars up to the border. It is the train in the Siege Question's satellite photos, with a 50 m shape under the tarpaulins.

nodes.t: Fission-powered crawler, prototype
nodes.x: A crawler the size of a city block, with a Pamir reactor, two Iskra turrets and a hangar of Mamonts. It has never moved more than a kilometre under its own power, and every bloc's satellites watch it try.

nodes.t: The first that can cross a border
nodes.x: A working Krepost, built for Moscow's push west into Europe: slow, close to unstoppable, and able to run its Iskras continuously off the reactor. It can't cross a river until engineers build it a bridge, and that's how its enemies know where it's going.

nodes.t: Where the Grafted Battalions were kept alive
nodes.x: Projected. On the North African Front the Safinas stop carrying Haboobs and start carrying the wounded. Their water plants and refineries are turned over to culture vats, and the grafts grown from the stolen cultures are fitted in their hangars, well behind the line. Each crawler becomes a sealed little world that keeps its people alive on its own water and its own tissue, and so does every ship Umoja builds after them. The Commonwealth keeps the name Safina for its carriers, and doesn't talk about what the crawlers grew.

nodes.t: Beijing's trains on lines Moscow never mapped
nodes.x: Projected. When the Pact splits, the Fortress Belt Railway turns to face west. Steppe outriders guide the trains along lines Moscow's planners never mapped, Tianshu reroutes them faster than the siege trains can follow, and Tieshan companies arrive at fights the Russians thought were days away. Beijing never stops building on the idea, and with the Tian Shan Rail wrecked in the war, it builds the next one where Steppe crews can guard it. In 2327 the line across Mongolia is the Ground to Orbit Accelerator, still run by Steppe crews, and it launches straight to orbit.

nodes.t: Bucket-wheel excavators and dragline rigs
nodes.x: Open-cast mining machines weighing thousands of tonnes, crawling a few hundred metres an hour. The largest land machines ever built.

nodes.t: Mining rigs as mobile frame depots
nodes.x: League mining companies parked old crawlers in the desert as workshops for militia frames. The Type-01Q's recoil dampers came out of them.

nodes.t: A mining crawler that carries a battalion
nodes.x: Qadira rebuilt a bucket-wheel crawler as a mobile base, with a hangar for eight Haboobs, a workshop, a water plant and a small refinery. It moves at 3 km/h and hides inside sandstorms. These are the League's capital ships.

nodes.t: Tracked rocket transporters
nodes.x: Huge, slow tracked platforms that carried rockets to the pad, and later carried cargo to the elevator anchors.

nodes.t: A swap point that drives itself
nodes.x: Bulwarks spend their lives seizing swap points, so the Army built one that brings itself: a launch-crawler chassis with Pitwagon bays, a turbine plant, and a Bulwark platoon riding on the roof. It's slow and impossible to hide, so it moves at night.

nodes.t: Lifting-body airships for remote freight
nodes.x: Helium hybrid airships that hauled mining gear to places with no roads. Slow and huge, they could set down on any flat ground.

nodes.t: An airship hangar for four Kestrels
nodes.x: America's first airborne carrier: a hybrid airship with a hangar gondola, swap bays, and turbine-driven fans to hold station. Kestrels launch by dropping out of the hangar and transforming. It's far too slow to survive anti-air fire, so it only works over the sea and empty desert.

nodes.t: The first helicarrier
nodes.x: Four ducted lift fans, turbines that burn fuel at a rate the Navy won't publish, and nine hours aloft. It carries eight Harriers and swaps their packs in the air. It's a carrier, not a warship: lightly armed and never taken within range of a fight. Only one exists.

nodes.t: Lift fans on beamed power
nodes.x: The Rookery refitted with a dorsal rectenna to run its lift fans on SKYLINE power. Under the relay it has stayed up for thirty hours. Outside the beam it has forty minutes, which sounds familiar.

nodes.t: Helicarriers in squadron service
nodes.x: Production helicarriers on HT-20 turbine-capacitor plants, topped up by SKYLINE wherever the relay reaches. Still carriers, not warships: any commander who takes one within range of a Mamont is relieved of command.

nodes.t: The first production warship built to fight in the air
nodes.x: A Rookery-class hull with an orbital warship's armour and catapults, lifted and powered by a fusion plant small enough to fly. The United States has never said where it got the reactor. The procurement file names the supplier as ██████ ████████ █████. It doesn't stay out of the fight: it carries a mass driver and laser batteries, and launches frames straight off its catapults.
nodes.z: War's end · the Lunar Mandate bans reactor-lifted ships from Earth's sky

nodes.t: Surplus cargo airships moving Gen 1 frames
nodes.x: League militias bought second-hand cargo airships to move frames across deserts with no roads. It worked until someone fired at one.
nodes.z: 2176 · too easy to shoot down in the Convoy Raids

nodes.t: Radar balloons over bases and borders
nodes.x: Tethered balloons that lift radars and radio relays high above bases, for far less than any aircraft costs.

nodes.t: OKB-7's Caspian sea-skimmers
nodes.x: Wing-in-ground-effect giants that fly a few metres above the Caspian at 500 km/h. Too strange to be ships and too low to be aircraft.

nodes.t: Flew Tieniu across the Caspian
nodes.x: A ground-effect craft with a nose door and a reinforced deck for two kneeling Tieniu. In the Caspian Crisis it landed frames on beaches in hours, where the landing ships needed days.

nodes.t: Ground-effect carrier for a Tieshan company
nodes.x: Bigger, faster, and armed with rocket racks. A Kaspiy-II can land a Tieshan company on any shore of an inland sea within the hour. It can't climb, so it can't cross land.

nodes.t: Fission-powered ground-effect cruiser
nodes.x: A Kaspiy hull with a Pamir reactor driving its fans. With unlimited power it can climb out of ground effect for minutes at a time, Moscow's first craft to fly with frames aboard instead of skimming. Every bloc worries about what happens if one comes down over a city.

nodes.t: Moscow's flying fortress
nodes.x: Kaspiy-Atom lift under a Krepost's armour and Iskra turrets. It flies low and slow, it's very hard to bring down, and it carries a full breakthrough group of Mamonts. If one is ever shot down, a reactor comes down with it.
nodes.z: War's end · the Lunar Mandate bans reactor-lifted ships from Earth's sky

nodes.t: “Ark”: a fusion-lifted rescue carrier
nodes.x: The Amaterasu reactor was too big for any normal frame, so Japan built a ship around one. The Hakobune is officially an unarmed disaster-response ship, with a hospital deck, lift fans and eight rescue frames. Its hangar is also exactly the right size for Takemikazuchi. Its first flight is what convinced the other blocs that fusion could fly.

nodes.t: The Ark goes north to Vladivostok
nodes.x: Projected. When Japan falls into China's sphere, the Hakobune's crew fly it north before Beijing can claim it, with Mitsurugi engineers packed into the hospital deck, and set it down at the company's Vladivostok subsidiary. Moscow wants the reactor. The Nashik pilots want the ship, and in the end Moscow and Delhi let them have it. Under their Oath it stays what it was built to be: unarmed, and sent wherever people need digging out. The Mandate grounds it with every other reactor-lifted ship, so after the war it goes up instead, with the Nashik pilots and the Mitsurugi exiles, to Europa and Io. The Ashva Compact's Sentinel-class carriers are built around its hangar.

nodes.t: Tugs and supply craft at the elevators
nodes.x: Small orbital tugs that moved cargo between the elevator tops and the early stations.

nodes.t: Tugs that carry Lifters to the job
nodes.x: Tenders with open cradles for Lifter frames, taking work crews out to new station segments. In the Rivet Strike they became the workers' fleet.

nodes.t: Long-haul carriers for Rigger crews
nodes.x: Larger tenders that take Rigger crews out for weeks on salvage contracts, with a winch bay and crew quarters. The Tether Incident was fought from two of them.

nodes.t: The first warships in orbit
nodes.x: The first dedicated warships, with a mass driver along the spine and catapults for Marlinspike frames. Nobody has fought with them yet.

nodes.t: Carries frames down, can't climb back
nodes.x: A warship that carries frames down through re-entry and releases them in the upper atmosphere. It can't return to orbit on its own. Its armour and catapults are the template every atmospheric warship copies.

nodes.t: Frames for boarding, fighter craft for the long reach
nodes.x: By the war's last years every orbital fleet has learned that frames win boarding actions and close fights around stations, but are too slow for open space. The lunar yards' answer launches both: Marlinspike descendants off the catapults, and small fighter craft from a second deck. Every carrier in 2327 still does, and counts both as its fighters. After the Lunar Mandate the yards go on building it for the UN, and UNEL's Safeguard is its direct heir. No other power will build in a slipway the UN controls, so each goes back to the yards it started before the war, and within a generation each has carriers of its own: the Ironshield, the Longchao, the Luftkogge and the rest.

fleets.label: Space Fleets
fleets.intro: The navies of the space age, from the first warships of 2186 to the fleets of No Peace Past Luna in 2327. Every class in the No Peace Past Luna faction briefs appears in the last two columns: the older hulls still in service come from the late era, and the newest classes from 2327 itself. Where a brief gives game stats, the card shows them: C for combat, F for fighters (frames and fighter craft together) and T for troops. The generations in between are the ones the briefs only hint at, dead ends included, and everything after the first column is projected. The war-era orbital carriers also stay on the Carriers tab.
turns: Warships before anyone can use them
The lunar yard builds catapult cruisers for every bloc. Nobody has fought ship to ship yet.
A single British dreadnought breaks the Russian inner fleet. Every navy spends the next century building dreadnoughts of its own.
Every power builds its own yards
The Lunar Mandate keeps Luna's slipways for the UN, so the powers build yards in their own orbits, and their ships stop looking alike.
Colonies start out with their sponsors' old hulls: American ships on northern Mars, Union ships in the south, Chinese ships in the Belt. Their own designs replace them one class at a time.
fams: Frames and fighter craft, launched together.

nodes.t: Armed tenders from the Rivet Strike
nodes.x: The station militias never fully disarmed after the Rivet Strike. Their tugs and tenders, with cutting gear and rivet guns bolted on, are the nearest thing to an escort in orbit.

nodes.t: Hull sections thrown up the Tian Shan
nodes.x: The Pact's first hulls of its own are built on the ground in sections small enough for the Tian Shan Rail, launched one at a time and bolted together in orbit. They are small, cramped and very cheap. In the war both halves of the Pact build them until the rail is wrecked.
nodes.z: The war · the rail is wrecked on the Central Asian front, and relaid under inspection after the Mandate

nodes.t: The Union's docks inside the Republic
nodes.x: The Union's leased docks on Malapert Mountain build frigates through the war, under the Lunar Guard's eye and on the Union's own designs. The same docks build the dreadnought that wins at Yernon. After the Mandate they are the only bloc docks inside UN jurisdiction.

nodes.t: Interceptor and scout, Latin subfaction
nodes.x: A very fast corvette with two light coilguns and missile rails, at its best in wolf packs: screening convoys, marking targets and chasing raiders. Latin-heritage crews paint their hulls, pick dramatic call-signs and fly riskier than they should. Colony One still runs a few as heritage pieces.

nodes.t: Clandestine rebuild
nodes.x: One of the classes Colony One's remnant builds in hidden docks beyond the main lanes. None has been deployed openly: if the United States thought the colony had rebuilt a navy, it would come to finish the job.

nodes.t: Escorts paid for by the megacorporations
nodes.x: The American corporations that kept the war effort supplied buy escorts of their own to guard their shipping. They want hulls that are cheap to run and easy to trust, which is still what the Ballista is.

nodes.t: Dependable escort, Latin subfaction
nodes.x: Three or four medium coilguns, a point-defence grid, and very little that breaks. Corporate fleets ran them through the war because they were cheap to keep, and they are still easy to maintain and easy to trust, if not as tough as Chinese or Union frigates.

nodes.t: Sleek, standardised, corporate-built
nodes.x: The Constitutionalists' picket: American-derived, contractor-built, and wired to fight alongside US forces rather than alone.

nodes.t: Raiders under a new flag every voyage
nodes.x: Grey Lantern sells the war a navy of privateers: fast, disguised raiders that hunt anyone's freighters for anyone's fee. Their tricks outlive the company. False transponders, hidden guns and ships that look like something else turn up in half the navies of 2327.

nodes.t: Reactor-fed lasers on a picket hull
nodes.x: The Navy tries pickets armed only with the reactor-fed lasers that once guarded its Harrier carriers. In vacuum they shed heat so slowly that they can fire for minutes, not hours.
nodes.z: Retired · once coilguns got cheap, nobody wanted a ship that had to wait to cool

nodes.t: Deterrence and local defence
nodes.x: A modernised American hull for local defence and showing the flag. Like the rest of the Constitutional fleet, it can't be sent to war without Washington's approval.

nodes.t: The Ballista's replacement, built for brickwork repairs
nodes.x: Thick, patchwork-friendly armour and three or four medium coilguns, built for the fast, ugly fixes Martian yards are good at. Martian crews love them; Earth engineers would have a heart attack. The remnant still builds them in secret.

nodes.t: The Mongolian outriders go up
nodes.x: The Steppe crews who guided Beijing's trains in the Pact Civil War go up through the Ground to Orbit Accelerator. Their light, fast craft scout ahead of China's expeditions into the Belt.

nodes.t: Outrider and scout, Steppe subfaction
nodes.x: Light and very fast, with agile vectoring for swarming. It is weaker than American or Union corvettes, but better at not being hit. Many have been sold into the Belt, where they serve as couriers and are slowly being replaced by Skyblades.

nodes.t: The backbone of the caravan escorts
nodes.x: Two coilguns and a modular rack on a very fast, nimble hull, kept polished like a racehorse. Skyblades guard convoys, hunt pirates and are replacing the Belt's old Steppewinds.

nodes.t: The Belt houses arm their tenders
nodes.x: The Belt's prospecting families bolt guns onto their tenders to stop claim-jumpers, then build faster hulls for nothing else. Every Skyblade crew can name the cutter its house started with.

nodes.t: The most dangerous frigate in the system
nodes.x: Four or five medium coilguns, two micro-fighters or drones, and the speed to flank, strike and leave. Steppe crews treat them like living horses. The Belt caravans prize the ones they can buy.

nodes.t: Built to treaty, crewed by many nations
nodes.x: The refounded Union builds escorts that comply with every treaty it signs: low emissions, careful fire control and room for inspectors.

nodes.t: Patrol and picket, Dutch subfaction
nodes.x: Low-emission and careful, with excellent sensor discipline. Fluyts are built to avoid trouble rather than start it. The Martian Research Directorate inherited some and keeps them for courier work until its own corvettes are ready.

nodes.t: Long-range scout frigate, Portuguese subfaction
nodes.x: Four medium coilguns and very good navigation. Not as deadly as a Windchaser, but steadier and more fuel-efficient. The Martian Research Directorate uses inherited Caravelas to fill out its screens until there are enough Redlines.

nodes.t: Calculation-first skirmisher
nodes.x: The Directorate's own frigate: fast, cold-running, and built around predictive fire control that improves the longer it watches a target. Its captains tend to come from orbital mechanics and prefer simulated duels to live drills.

nodes.t: Armed tugs on the Orbital Front
nodes.x: In the war every fleet needs ships cheaper than a cruiser to watch the lanes, chase raiders and screen convoys. The lunar yards build armed pickets by the hundred, and most escort classes still in service in 2327 descend from them.

nodes.t: The lunar crews' pickets, under the UN
nodes.x: After the Lunar Mandate the lunar crews' pickets become the UN's patrol fleet. They enforce exclusion zones and escort relief convoys between Earth and Luna.

nodes.t: Orbital patrol, Earth subfaction
nodes.x: The backbone of UNEL's patrols, built to intercept unsafe traffic and stop other people's fights from spreading. Its crews come mostly from civil-service families.

nodes.t: Exclusion-zone enforcer, Luna subfaction
nodes.x: Three precision coilguns, ablative plating and a thermal damping suite for working in lunar shadow. Arbiters are built to end fights, not chase them.

nodes.t: Escort for relief convoys
nodes.x: A fast escort for relief convoys and evacuation lanes, named, like the Tunis Works frames, for a desert wind.

nodes.t: Patrol frigate with a hospital bay
nodes.x: Guards shipping lanes and outlying settlements, and carries a hospital bay most navies would give to a transport.

nodes.t: Picket and courier
nodes.x: Fast and lightly armed, sent ahead of every Ascendancy formation.

nodes.t: The first ships built for Jupiter
nodes.x: The Nashik exiles' first warships at Europa and Io are cutters armoured against Jupiter's radiation more than against weapons. They pull crews out of failing habitats far more often than they fight.

nodes.t: Raider-hunter
nodes.x: Escorts convoys along the Ascendancy's extraction routes and hunts the raiders who prey on them.

nodes.t: Habitat picket
nodes.x: A small, self-repairing picket that guards Umoja's habitats and seed shipments. Its hull composites heal the way its crews do.

nodes.t: Biological security patrol
nodes.x: Umoja's patrol frigate, with sealed life-support and quarantine bays. Its first job is keeping anything alive and uninvited away from Ganymede.

nodes.t: Route patrol, named for the sworn pilots
nodes.x: Armoured for radiation and debris, and sent to anyone in trouble on the Jovian routes. The class takes its name from the Nashik pilots' oath name for themselves.

nodes.t: Convoy defence
nodes.x: A heavy frigate for convoy defence and route control, with the endurance to stay on station through Jupiter's radiation.

nodes.t: Stealthy courier
nodes.x: A cold-running courier that carries messages and pilgrims between the Communion's scattered habitats without being seen.

nodes.t: Insulated long-range escort
nodes.x: A sparse, cold-hardened frigate built for very long voyages far from any dock. Pilgrims rarely gather in numbers, and when they do, it seems to have been arranged.

nodes.t: Cargo between the elevator tops, the Moon and Mars
nodes.x: Ascension's freighters, then the Republic's and the blocs', move cargo from the elevator tops to the stations and the Moon. One of them carried Colony One's settlers to Mars.

nodes.t: Keeping the Moon and Mars supplied
nodes.x: Through the war the lunar crews keep freighters running to Luna and to a colony on Mars that Earth has stopped paying attention to. Colony One grows up on what they bring.

nodes.t: Modular hauler, Latin subfaction
nodes.x: Found everywhere from Luna to the Belt, with deeply modular cargo, troop and science bays. Its name is a corruption of leyenda. Colony One fits its Veyendas out as homes.

nodes.t: Contractor-built logistics
nodes.x: The Constitutionalists' transport, built and serviced by the American contractors who run most of their logistics.

nodes.t: The ships that put Colony One on Mars
nodes.x: Landers built in Ascension's last years set Colony One down in the north, and an unannounced camp in Melas Chasma months later. Colony One's own transports are still built around their life support.

nodes.t: The mother ship of Colony One's fleet
nodes.x: Long-duration life support and sealed biosystems tuned to Martian physiology, for moving troops and habitats and evacuating the wounded. Crews paint settlement murals on its walls.

nodes.t: Belt water, routed by Tianshu
nodes.x: Automated haulers bring Belt ice and ore inward on routes Tianshu plans years ahead. Their crews are few and their holds are huge, and when one wears out, someone always buys the hull.

nodes.t: “Black Star”: the backbone of Chinese logistics
nodes.x: Highly automated cargo and troop handling lets it run on a reduced crew. In the Belt it is the most common bulk hauler, carrying ore, migrants and whole clans in cramped quarters.

nodes.t: Aid and reconstruction, French subfaction
nodes.x: Built for habitability and crew welfare over capacity, and often carrying more inspectors than soldiers. The Martian Research Directorate uses inherited Fusiliers between its settlements.

nodes.t: An army moved at once
nodes.x: A bulk transport for troops, colonists and their machines. It inherits the siege trains' job of moving a whole army at once.

nodes.t: Reconstruction cargo for a damaged Earth
nodes.x: The UN's first new hulls after the Mandate carry reconstruction cargo, refugees and relief down to Earth's orbit. Crews start calling them arks.

nodes.t: UNEL's humanitarian flagship class
nodes.x: Carries troops, refugees, medical cargo or reconstruction modules, with the best environmental control in the system and almost no guns. Earth crews call Providences arks, after the relief ships before them.

nodes.t: Armoured evacuation ship
nodes.x: Heavily armoured for radiation and debris, and built to get a whole habitat's people out when something breaks.

nodes.t: Water, feedstock, refugees, whole communities
nodes.x: Named for the League convoys that kept the Jinn supplied. It moves water, feedstock, refugees and, when it has to, whole communities.

nodes.t: A sealed ecology that travels
nodes.x: A transport that carries its own biosphere, so colonists, crops and livestock arrive alive across Jovian distances.

nodes.t: Anything that will fly, leaving Earth
nodes.x: After the war, people who no longer trust any government on Earth leave in whatever will reach orbit and keep them alive: old freighters, worn-out ice haulers, stripped transports. The descendants of the ice communities are among them.

nodes.t: A wandering habitat-ship
nodes.x: Part transport and part settlement, able to survive for years with no outside support. What it carries is often holy as well as useful.

nodes.t: The first warships, 2186
nodes.x: The Lunar Republic's yard builds the first dedicated warships for every bloc: a mass driver along the spine and catapults for Marlinspike frames. Every carrier and battleship in this tree descends from them.

nodes.t: Frames for boarding, fighter craft for the long reach
nodes.x: In the war the lunar yards' carriers learn to launch both: frames for boarding actions and fights around stations, fighter craft for open space. Every carrier since counts both as its fighters.

nodes.t: The lunar crews' carriers, under the UN
nodes.x: After the Lunar Mandate the yards go on building the mixed-wing design for the UN alone, with interceptor bays and room for relief cargo.

nodes.t: Peacekeeping carrier, Luna subfaction
nodes.x: Modular bays for interceptors, aid drones and research craft. Less armoured than an Ironshield but far more efficient, and crewed by lunar flyers proud of precise flying and minimal waste.

nodes.t: Frames down through re-entry, and no way back
nodes.x: Built to release frames in the upper atmosphere, and unable to climb back to orbit alone. Their armour and catapults are copied by every atmospheric warship.
nodes.z: War's end · the Mandate closes the lanes down to Earth

nodes.t: The Navy's flat deck goes to orbit
nodes.x: Barred from Earth's sky and unwilling to rent Luna's slipways, the United States builds its carriers at Hampton Roads, the orbital dockyard it started before the war, and builds them to look like the supercarriers they replace.

nodes.t: Fortress carrier, core fleet
nodes.x: Built to survive everything except subtlety, with dense point defence and the largest fighter wing in the system. It deliberately echoes the old supercarriers: flat deck, rugged angles, industrial pride. Colony One keeps a few as deterrents.

nodes.t: Corporate-integrated carrier
nodes.x: An American-derived carrier with contractor-built support systems and command architecture for working alongside US forces. Built for deterrence and political signalling, not for a war it fights alone.

nodes.t: Fighters run on beamed power
nodes.x: A carrier whose fighters fly on power beamed from orbital relays: the SKYLINE idea taken into space. It needs fewer fuel stores and far more trust in the relays.
nodes.z: Abandoned · a carrier that needs a relay can be switched off from somewhere else

nodes.t: Surplus war hulls refitted for Mars
nodes.x: Colony One's first carriers are worn-out war hulls the Americans no longer want, refitted at Phobos. They are too hungry for parts and crew to keep forever, and Colony One designs the Dustwing to replace them.

nodes.t: Half an Ironshield, built for Mars
nodes.x: A compact carrier with fewer crew, simpler repairs and room to double as a lab or a transport, built from Phobos Forgeworks frames. The remnant still builds them in secret. “We don't need to outgun Earth. We just need to outlast it.”

nodes.t: Tianshu-run decks
nodes.x: China's first carriers are built in sections on the ground, launched by rail and built around Tianshu: fewer crew, more drones, and rotation control the American ships never match.

nodes.t: “Dragon Nest”: balanced and crew-efficient
nodes.x: Less armoured than an Ironshield but more adaptable, with fourteen to sixteen fighters or strike drones and exceptional rotation control.

nodes.t: Carriers with no pilots aboard
nodes.x: Beijing's first answer to fighter craft is a tender full of Tianshu-flown drones. The drones are good; the tenders are fragile. Their drone bays go into the Longchao, where strike drones still share the deck with piloted fighters.

nodes.t: Holds big enough to be hangars
nodes.x: Emptied, a Belt ore carrier's hold can take a squadron. Caravans carry their own fighters in them long before anyone calls the result a carrier.

nodes.t: Carriers as markets and courts
nodes.x: Chinese carriers traded into the Belt in debt settlements become caravan flagships: mobile markets, arbitration courts and convoy commands. The houses care more about the hangar space than the fighters.

nodes.t: A home away from home for Syndicate pilots
nodes.x: Huge hangars and room for a large marine complement, paid for with armour. The Goldpurse lets its money do the talking. The Belt's prestige carriers are still Longchaos.

nodes.t: Command ships first, carriers second
nodes.x: The refounded Union builds carriers to run multinational task groups, the way its Lance Transports once ran a lance. Each one carries a fleet staff before it carries fighters.

nodes.t: Mid-weight carrier, German subfaction
nodes.x: Reliable and sometimes over-engineered, with a strong defensive grid. Union doctrine treats it as a command centre first and a weapons platform second.

nodes.t: Inherited Luftkogges, reworked on Deimos
nodes.x: The Martian Research Directorate inherits Union carriers and spends decades learning what it would change: the hangars, the refit system and the command architecture.

nodes.t: The thinking carrier
nodes.x: Adaptive hangars reconfigure its fighters between missions, and layered energy shielding stands in for armour. Its decks feel halfway between a warship and a research lab.

nodes.t: Prototype
nodes.x: The Martian Research Directorate's next carrier, still in prototype. The Directorate's remaining Luftkogges are to be phased out in its favour.

nodes.t: Lunar hulls refitted for evacuation
nodes.x: The Commonwealth's first carriers are bought from the lunar yards and refitted with hospital decks and water plants, like the Safina crawlers before them.

nodes.t: Named for the League's capital ships
nodes.x: Built like the mining crawlers it is named for, with hangars, workshops, a water plant and a hospital deck. Its fighters fly cover for evacuations as often as they fight.

nodes.t: Grown as much as built
nodes.x: Umoja's first carriers grow out of the Commonwealth's relief carriers and the grafting knowledge that went to Jupiter. Their hulls repair themselves.

nodes.t: A carrier that feels like an organism
nodes.x: Self-repair systems, biotech composites and sealed ecological architecture. Its doctrine is habitat defence, but its hangars hold units other powers find hard to look at.

nodes.t: The Tsitadel's doctrine, in orbit
nodes.x: Grounded by the Mandate, Moscow's fortress idea goes up: a carrier that keeps its fighters inside its armour.

nodes.t: A fortress that carries its fighters inside
nodes.x: Named for the legendary city that sank beneath a lake rather than be taken. Every crew member has an escape craft.

nodes.t: The Ark that went up
nodes.x: The Hakobune never flies in Earth's sky again after the Mandate, but it reaches Europa with the Nashik pilots and the Mitsurugi exiles. Its hangar is still the Compact's model for a carrier.

nodes.t: Built around the Hakobune's hangar
nodes.x: A carrier for rescue, convoy defence and habitat security, armoured for Jupiter's radiation. When one arrives, people believe someone might hold the line.

nodes.t: Whole communities in the dark
nodes.x: The ice communities' descendants leave in habitat-ships that carry everything they need, a long way from anyone else. Their first carriers are habitat-ships with hangars.

nodes.t: Named for the carrier frozen in at Ellesmere
nodes.x: A long-range habitat-carrier for the coldest places in the system. The Communion names it after the Polar Carrier that kept its ancestors alive.

nodes.t: Mass-driver battleships for whoever is buying
nodes.x: The lunar yards stretch the catapult cruisers into line ships with heavier mass drivers, and sell them to any side that can pay, though by the second year of the war every great power is building its own.

nodes.t: Guns over boarding strength
nodes.x: The first battleships from America's own yards: heavy coilguns, heavy armour and small troop decks.

nodes.t: America's line-of-battle workhorse
nodes.x: Six to eight heavy coilguns, extreme durability, and a smaller troop deck than the Martian Research Directorate's or the Union's ships. Unofficial motto: “Steel over silicone. Fire over finesse.” Colony One uses its few as escorts.

nodes.t: The Constitutional capital ship
nodes.x: A modernised American-derived battleship, built for deterrence and interoperability with US forces.

nodes.t: The remnant's hidden capital ship
nodes.x: Built in the Black Docks and not yet shown in the open. If it ever is, the United States will know Colony One has rebuilt a navy.

nodes.t: Precision over weight
nodes.x: Beijing's battleships trade weight of fire for Tianshu-coordinated precision and good frigate screens.

nodes.t: “Divine Blade”: the finesse battleship
nodes.x: Six heavy coilguns and a precision-targeting suite. It hits softer than other battleships, so Chinese doctrine wins with AI-coordinated fire and better frigates. Wealthy Belt clans keep a few as prestige ships.

nodes.t: The Syndicate's first true capital ship
nodes.x: Strong enough to deter raids, cheap enough for a rich caravan, and modular enough to refit for trade war. Few caravans can afford one without great fortune.

nodes.t: Guns hidden in the cargo holds
nodes.x: Caravans tired of raiders fit heavy guns inside ordinary freighters and wait to be attacked. The Fortune's modular trade-war refits come from them.

nodes.t: Fleet cohesion over bravado
nodes.x: Balanced line ships with strong mid-range firepower, built to fight as part of a fleet.

nodes.t: Dependable line ship, Spanish subfaction
nodes.x: Thick forward plating and good endurance. Less punch than a Thunderbreak, but easier to keep running. The Martian Research Directorate uses inherited Galeóns for shows of force.

nodes.t: The most accurate battleship in the system
nodes.x: Built to set the geometry of a fight from stand-off range. Several Axioms can share targeting in real time. Its captains are austere and almost devout about optimal solutions.

nodes.t: Presence, not fear
nodes.x: The UN's battleships exist to anchor negotiations and declare jurisdiction, and are built to last rather than to trade blows.

nodes.t: A mobile courtroom
nodes.x: Six heavy coilguns, very clean exhaust and systems built for long deployments. Its captains often come from diplomacy or civil government.

nodes.t: Armour forward, civilians behind
nodes.x: The Commonwealth's first battleships are built to hold a position while civilians get clear behind them.

nodes.t: The Commonwealth's line of battle
nodes.x: Heavily armoured forward and built to hold a position while civilians get clear.

nodes.t: Habitat defence
nodes.x: Umoja's capital ship, built to stand between its habitats and anything that threatens their ecology.

nodes.t: Broken at Yernon
nodes.x: Moscow's line ships, assembled in orbit from sections thrown up the Tian Shan Rail, hold the inner lanes until the Battle of Yernon, where a single British dreadnought breaks them. The Ascendancy builds every battleship since with that day in mind.

nodes.t: America's first hulls from its own yard
nodes.x: The first American hulls from Hampton Roads come out in the war's last year: too late to matter at Yernon, just in time to matter afterwards. Every American line ship and carrier since has been built in the same yard.

nodes.t: The Krepost idea, in orbit
nodes.x: After Yernon, Moscow's planners build the biggest guns they can on hulls that barely move: siege monitors to hold the lanes.
nodes.z: Scrapped · they never caught anything that could run

nodes.t: Slow, and very hard to kill
nodes.x: Named for the warrior heroes of Russian epic. Heavily compartmented, with a way out from every station.

nodes.t: Named for the field of the great war
nodes.x: A heavily armoured battleship for decisive intervention on the Jovian routes, named for the battlefield of the Mahabharata.

nodes.t: The Communion's rare heavy ship
nodes.x: Cold-hardened and long-ranged, and seldom seen. When Testaments do appear, it is usually by arrangement.

nodes.t: The ship that won Yernon
nodes.x: A British dreadnought from the Union's Malapert docks arrives alone at the Battle of Yernon and breaks the Russian inner fleet. A Union written off since the European Front is a great power again, and every navy wants dreadnoughts.

nodes.t: The Senior Service has no rival in the void
nodes.x: Ten to twelve heavy guns, long-range precision cannon and a dense point-defence grid. The British kept the name to remind humanity who invented the concept. The Martian Research Directorate keeps its inherited Dreadnoughts indefinitely.

nodes.t: Sent only when protecting someone means facing a fleet
nodes.x: Named for the ancient capital of Kush, downriver from Khartoum. Few are built.

nodes.t: Dreadnoughts built in a hurry
nodes.x: Within a decade of Yernon every navy has rushed out dreadnoughts of its own. The American ones are the biggest and the worst: heavy, unreliable and expensive to crew.
nodes.z: Scrapped · under UNEL arms reduction, which few navies minded by then

nodes.t: Sustained fire, fielded in numbers
nodes.x: Eight to ten ultra-heavy coilguns and a spinal rail cannon. Less monstrous than Union or Chinese dreadnoughts, but more versatile. Every crew member must be unmodified. Colony One runs its few sparingly.

nodes.t: “Heaven's Fury”: a monastic artillery temple
nodes.x: Ten to twelve ultra-heavy coilguns tuned with AI targeting harmonics. Its crews take cognitive optimisation to work with the targeting AI. Some have ended up in the Belt through debt settlements.

nodes.t: A bank vault and a courtroom
nodes.x: Built for long, lonely voyages as a trade-route anchor and neutral court. It has three bridges: one to fly the ship, one to count the money, and one to negotiate marriages.

nodes.t: Lunar guardians that never leave
nodes.x: The UN's first heavy ships are monitors parked over Luna's poles, watching the lanes from fixed stations. The Pillar is what they become once someone decides they should be able to move.

nodes.t: Slow, immovable, hard to overwhelm
nodes.x: Hardened lunar composites, a spinal coil projector and the Custodian Array, a long-duration monitoring suite named for the lunar yard's giant. Its crews are almost monastic.

nodes.t: The answer to Yernon
nodes.x: Named for Vishnu's discus. No single enemy ship is meant to break an Ascendancy fleet again.

nodes.t: Umoja's largest living ship
nodes.x: Dense with self-repair systems and sealed ecological architecture. Few powers want to find out what its hangars hold.

nodes.t: The Compact's heaviest ship
nodes.x: Named for the Slavic thunder god, and built to hold the Jovian line when nothing smaller can.

orgs.label: Organisations
orgs.intro: The companies, laboratories and institutions behind everything else in the atlas, placed in the era where each first matters. Lines show what each grew out of, bought into or reacted against. Select one to see the machines, conflicts and doctrine it's tied to.
turns: Every mech maker began as something else: Halcyon built jets, Brannock-Hale tanks, Tianlong excavators, OKB-7 interceptors, Mitsurugi rescue robots. Their old products still show in every frame they build.
The Partnership Act let Brannock-Hale and Halcyon design, build, crew and maintain their own frames. It was meant to be temporary. Their lobbyists wrote most of its renewals.
Halden, Department Zero, Tsukuyomi Lab and Vireo all begin their work in the same decade, and none of them answers to a parliament.

An ethics panel that can stop a program, a lunar yard sworn to no bloc, keepers who won't command what they care for, a UN that has started bringing its own frames. The organisations that outlast the war are the ones that learned to say no.
fams: The US, Union and Canadian companies behind the West's frames.
State combines, design bureaus and Japan's capacitor maker.
From desert workshops to two design offices of Africa's own.
A consortium, its workers, and the houses beyond its reach.
Geneva's agencies, its borrowed white frames, and the institution the war forces on everyone.
Where the supers were made, and the bodies that answer for them.
Mercenaries, miners, and a canal that started opening containers.

nodes.t: Fighter maker turned frame maker
nodes.x: America's fighter and ground-attack jet maker before mechs, and the source of every Halcyon frame's wing binders, avionics and flight-control software. It licensed Brannock's Garrison as the Sparrowhawk, then built the variable frames that defined US doctrine: the Merlin, the Kestrel and the Harrier. Since the Partnership Act it designs, builds, crews and maintains its own frames, and its engineers hold reserve commissions.

nodes.t: Tanks, construction walkers, then the Garrison
nodes.x: America's tank and heavy-equipment maker. It put a construction walker's legs under a tank's armour and built the first mech to see combat, the M4 Garrison, which nearly everyone has licensed, copied or rebuilt since. The Army's frames are Brannock's, from the Teamster to the Bulwark, and so is most of the Army's lobbying.

nodes.t: The Union's frame maker
nodes.x: A European maker of armoured reconnaissance vehicles whose sensor masts and quiet running shaped every frame it built. It licence-built the Garrison as the Écuyer, then designed the standard-hardpoint Haubert that the Union's modular doctrine rests on.

nodes.t: Cold-weather frames from between the blocs
nodes.x: Canada's maker of snow tractors and ice-road haulers, then of frames: first licensed Garrisons built in Calgary, then its own Arctic designs on US chassis with Union sensors. It sells to Norway as readily as to Ottawa, and builds on both sides of a line nobody has drawn yet.

nodes.t: Brannock-Hale and Halcyon, chartered by Congress
nodes.x: The joint venture Congress chartered to do what neither company could alone: build the Concord. It took the first full-scale HT-20 plant, Bulwark armour and Harrier avionics to 40 m. About a dozen Concords later, some of its parts have left its depots on paperwork nobody can trace.

nodes.t: A workers' cooperative in a squatted hangar
nodes.x: Founded in 2172 by Kassel engineers and Blitz crews who walked out when Vauclair-Ehrlich standardised on the Haubert and scrapped every Blitz. They squatted a disused hangar at Tempelhof and registered as a cooperative, so that no consortium could ever buy them. They named themselves for the callsign of the last Blitz pair still running in the Maghreb Depot Strikes. Every member has one vote and every drawing is published, and the Union procurement office has never enjoyed a meeting with them. The German contingents buy their frames anyway. In 2185 a narrow vote took a contract from Berlin itself, and the cooperative split over it. The thirty-nine percent took the Querschläger drawings to Mongolia.

nodes.t: Herder-mechanics, then Berlin's splinter
nodes.x: Named for the wind horse on the prayer flags. It began around 2175 as a cooperative of rail workshops in Darkhan, building the fast frames for the Steppe outriders that Tianlong wouldn't. In 2185 a few hundred Funkenwerk members who walked out over the Berlin contract joined it. It still holds one vote per member, now in three languages. Berlin calls that desertion; they call it the same vote they always held. Beijing tolerates them because the outriders vouch for them and Tianshu can't predict them, which Beijing has decided is useful.

nodes.t: Hand-built frames for named aces
nodes.x: An Italian atelier that builds a handful of frames a year on Vauclair-Ehrlich bones, each for one named ace: the Falco, the Saetta, and now Roland, the only super the ethics panel has approved. Its racing stacks run at 140% of rated output, and its paint is always red and gold. It opened a workshop beside the Tunis line and built the Ghibli there.

nodes.t: A frame line in Mexico
nodes.x: The Monterrey Accords' industrial half: a Brannock-Hale line building Teamsters in Monterrey with Mexican crews. When Mexico joins the United States in the war, it becomes one of the country's largest frame plants overnight.

nodes.t: The Navy's yard, rebuilt in orbit
nodes.x: Named for the Norfolk navy yard the sea took. Joint Heavy Systems is building it at the L1 point so the US Navy never has to rent a lunar slipway again. In 2186 it is one frame, a skeleton crew and a schedule nobody believes. It is finished during the war, and every American orbital carrier since has been built there.

nodes.t: European slipways, leased inside the Republic
nodes.x: Strasbourg's answer to the lunar yard: docks of its own on Malapert Mountain, leased from the Republic and crewed by Union engineers. The Lunar Guard inspects them, and the Union argues about it in eleven languages. In the war they build the dreadnought that wins at Yernon. After the Mandate they are the only bloc docks inside UN jurisdiction, which is part of why the Transatlantic Union stays UNEL's closest partner.

nodes.t: One company, two countries
nodes.x: Projected. When Canada splits, Boreal splits with it: the Calgary plant builds for the United States and the Montreal plant for the Union, and the two companies trade patents through lawyers in Iceland. Each built half of the Aurora, and neither can build the whole.

nodes.t: Excavators, tractors, then the most-built mech in the world
nodes.x: Beijing's state machinery combine. Its excavators and tractors gave the Tieniu its drive train, and its factories built the Tieshan in thousands and now the Jingwei in series. It runs the frame trains and, through its orbital subsidiary, the prospecting tenders. It also built the network that now plans its wars.

nodes.t: A fighter bureau that builds heavy frames
nodes.x: A Moscow design bureau that built interceptors and bombers before mechs, and carried their heavy, aggressive engineering into the Medved, the Mamont and the Tsar. It opened a second line at Nashik, builds the Staya's wolves, and houses a department that officially does not exist.

nodes.t: Rescuers first, then the world's capacitors
