nodes.x: Japan's disaster-robotics and industrial-capacitor maker. Its capacitor cores are inside nearly every linear and energy weapon in the world, and licensing them to everyone is Japan's real defence doctrine.

nodes.t: A rail scheduler that learned to plan wars
nodes.x: Tianlong's logistics program for the frame trains, and the first time the Pact let software decide where its frames went. It grew into the planner behind the Fortress Belt, cued the Air Umbrella, and under Order 21 drafts every operational plan for officers to approve. In 2184 it named Moscow as the second front.

nodes.t: OKB-7's Indian line
nodes.x: The price of the Delhi Accession: an OKB-7 factory at Nashik building Medveds under Russian supervision, with engineers who rebuilt the cooling twice before Moscow agreed it needed rebuilding. Its first clean-sheet design, the Ashvin, is built around the Nashik Oath.

nodes.t: Archives copied, just in case
nodes.x: Registered quietly after Beijing's customs began holding Japanese capacitor shipments. On paper they are sales offices. In practice Mitsurugi has copied its design archives to both, and their staff lists are mostly engineers.

nodes.t: The Pact's own road to orbit
nodes.x: A magnetic launch track that climbs forty kilometres up the Tian Shan and throws hull sections into orbit, where Pact crews bolt them together. Tianlong built the track and Tianshu times the launches; OKB-7 builds the hull sections. Both General Staffs claim it, and in the war it becomes the most fought-over forty kilometres in Central Asia. It is wrecked there, and relaid after the Mandate under UN inspection.

nodes.t: Engineers who left before the factory was taken
nodes.x: Projected. When Japan falls into China's sphere, the subsidiaries take engineers, archives and actuator lines out with them. The Ohio half is absorbed into American industry. The Vladivostok half goes a long way further, and its actuators end up in the Ashva Compact.

nodes.t: Building to European licence
nodes.x: Shipyards and rail works that built ferries, rolling stock and tractors under French and Italian licence for most of a century, and kept the old Carthaginian habit of trading with everyone.

nodes.t: Militia garages and mining crawlers
nodes.x: Before there was a League there were workshops: militia garages and mining companies' parked crawlers where surplus Garrisons and Tieniu were rebuilt with sand filters and whatever parts turned up. Every League frame starts in one.

nodes.t: Three blocs' parts on one frame
nodes.x: The League's frame maker, grown out of the desert workshops. Its frames take US, Union and Pact parts at once, and every part has a supplier in at least two blocs. Its refurbished cannons fire standing, which Tianlong never managed.

nodes.t: A Union Haubert plant for North African partners
nodes.x: Opened by Strasbourg after the Maghreb Depot Strikes to prove its partners would never again be left blind: a Haubert line run by French engineers, built and flown by Tunisian and Algerian crews. Castellani opened a workshop beside it.

nodes.t: The first frames designed in Africa
nodes.x: Qadira moved its design office to Khartoum the month the Charter was signed. Its first design, the Harmattan, is built to shelter people rather than hold ground.

nodes.t: The Charter's second design office
nodes.x: When the Maghreb signed the Khartoum Charter, the Tunis line went with it, and so did most of its French and Italian engineers. Under Qadira they are building the Elissa. Strasbourg has asked for its licences back. Tunis has not replied.

nodes.t: A workshop run by assembly
nodes.x: Projected. Moroccan mechanics and Southern Crossing volunteers, most of them Spanish and many of them Catalan, take over a shipbreaking yard, run it by assembly and build the Tramuntana from the North African Front's wreckage. The crew is elected and everyone eats at the same table.

nodes.t: The consortium that ran the elevators, until 2182
nodes.x: An orbital consortium jointly owned across the blocs, running the elevators, the solar ring and the stations. It launched the Ares mission, sealed ████ ████ ████ in Station Nine, armed its worker frames slowly, and in 2182 it came apart. Its lunar half merged with the lunar cities to become the Lunar Republic, which took the solar ring and the stations; the bloc shareholders, who no longer trusted each other, divided the elevators between them before the year was out.

nodes.t: Workers who were never fully disarmed
nodes.x: Formed in the Rivet Strike, when station workers armed their Lifters and held a station for a month. Ascension settled and never fully disarmed them. Their children crew the lunar yard and vote in the Lunar Republic, and in 2185 the militias became its Lunar Guard.

nodes.t: A sealed laboratory most of its owners think is a fuel depot
nodes.x: Ascension's high-orbit laboratory, built to hold ███ ████████. It sold, or lost, ███ ██████ ██████ ████ ████ ██████, went dark for nine hours the week H-17 woke, and sent the crew who are now digging at Melas Chasma.

nodes.t: Tianlong's prospecting subsidiary
nodes.x: The subsidiary that sent family-crewed tenders out to prospect near-Earth asteroids. Out there, Tianshu's plans arrive late and fit badly.

nodes.t: A foundry that became a state
nodes.x: Founded in 2182, when Ascension's lunar half merged with the councils of Shackleton, Malapert, Peary and Tranquility. It owns the yards, the ice and the lunar stations, and since Ascension was broken up the solar ring and the orbital stations too, and it lives by making what nobody on Earth can: vacuum-cast hulls, lunar composites, coil weapons and beamed power. Its citizens are mostly Ascension engineers and their lunar-born children. It applied to join the UN within a week; the Council vetoed it, and the Assembly seated it as an observer. It has backed the UN with everything but a vote ever since: frames for the white squads, and relays parked over their operations. Since the Pressure War it also has a Lunar Guard, a First Speaker with emergency powers, and ice camps on the far side.

nodes.t: Luna's frames, built for Earth
nodes.x: The Republic's frame works, in the old Ascension worker-frame shops under Shackleton's rim, and the most advanced frame foundry anywhere. It builds for a gravity it doesn't have, tests in the Atacama, and sells to nobody: everything it makes for Earth goes to the UN as a gift, and every bloc's procurement office would pay for what it gives away. Its engineers are Earthward almost to a person.

nodes.t: Builds for every bloc, sworn to the Republic
nodes.x: The Republic's yard on the rim of Shackleton crater, and in 2186 the only slipway that can build a warship, so every bloc's first warships come off it while each bloc builds its own way up. Its engineers are citizens of the Republic and sworn to no bloc, and between contracts they are building the Custodian. The UN's vetoed orbital treaty is pinned up in the crew mess.

nodes.t: Luna exists for Earth
nodes.x: The Republic's governing faction, strongest among the Works' engineers and the old Ascension families. They hold that Luna owes the planet it came from, because space is dark and cold without it. They want the Republic inside the UN and its frames on Earth's side. Since Malapert they have also wanted the Lunar Guard.

nodes.t: Let the Earth burn
nodes.x: Mostly young and lunar-born, and named for the side of the Moon that never sees Earth. They say the planet is finished, the blocs will drag Luna down with it, and the Republic should sell its warships to the highest bidder and close the door. Since Malapert their leaders are in the far-side ice camps, and their cells meet in the pipes.

nodes.t: The office that stayed behind
nodes.x: When Ascension was broken up, one office never appeared on anyone's list of assets. It took Station Nine's staff with it and still trades under the old name. It charters the Melas camp, pays its crew through three shell freight companies, and reports to a board subcommittee whose membership is ███████████. Halden's Mars proposal was forwarded to it in 2186 and came back annotated: ██████ ████ ██ ███████████.

nodes.t: Contractors who keep their own books
nodes.x: The families crewing Tianlong's tenders keep their own ledgers, trade among themselves, settle disputes by reputation and buy continuity contracts to keep their elders. Beijing calls them contractors. They call themselves houses, and Beijing's charter makes them the Celestial Prosperity Syndicate.

nodes.t: Vetoed into a relief agency
nodes.x: Three blocs, three permanent vetoes, and a Security Council that has not passed a resolution any of them minded since before the Ares mission. The UN left New York for Geneva in the 2140s, after the flood barriers failed and Washington declined to pay for new ones. In 2165 it asked the blocs to sign a convention treating mechs as weapons of war; none did. What remains is a relief service, a climate ledger nobody reads and a General Assembly that votes for things the Council then vetoes. Its staff keep counting the drowned coasts and failing harvests anyway.

nodes.t: Borrowed frames, painted white
nodes.x: The UN has no army and no frame maker, so its frames are whatever members will give it: ex-mining walkers, surplus Garrisons and Teamsters, Brazilian Hauberts, a Tieshan bought second-hand from Bolivia, Kizunas lent by Japan. Each is stripped of its bloc's markings, painted white, and given a blue head. A squad is four to six frames that share no parts, crewed by volunteers seconded from Brazil, Ghana, Ireland, Mongolia, Norway and New Zealand, and its mechanics are the best scavengers in any army. The crews call themselves blueheads. Their rules let them fire only to protect a convoy, a camp or themselves. At Mong Hsat they fired first.

nodes.n: United Nations of Earth and Luna
nodes.t: The institution that ends the war
nodes.x: Projected. When the war turns atomic, the Lunar Republic puts the yards, the ring and every ship it crews under the United Nations, the one institution every side had ignored through the war and still let into the ruins, and closes the lanes to Earth until the blocs stop fighting. Geneva's relief agencies become the Office of Global Stewardship; the white squads and the lunar fleets become the Directorate of Unified Security, and the Republic's Assembly becomes its lunar chamber. What comes out of it has its own navy and a mandate few asked for and none could refuse.

nodes.t: ███████ tissue, Union money, now on trial
nodes.x: A Geneva research institute that bought tissue ████ ███████ ████, or stole it, and spent a decade learning to grow it into giants whose pilots are chosen to be leashes. Since the Great Sand Sea its laboratories have been the ethics panel's first case, and its surviving scientists have proposed the one program the panel might approve.

nodes.t: Officially does not exist
nodes.x: OKB-7's secret institute for augmented pilots, run from Moscow and funded through a budget line that reads ████████ ████ ███████. It began with neural-interface trials on volunteers who were not always volunteers, built the Koschei, and lost one of its pilots off the range. Beijing wants it shut down. After the war, the Ascendancy closes it.

nodes.t: A weather office with a reactor licence
nodes.x: Listed in Pact registers as a meteorological bureau. It holds the only Pact licence for portable fission plants, shares a perimeter fence with an OKB-7 test range, and is funded through Department Zero's ████████ ████ line. The Pamir's reactor carries its stamp. Delhi's liaison officers have asked to visit. None has been cleared.

nodes.t: Mitsurugi's black-projects laboratory
nodes.x: The lab behind the BX-0, the Raijin and the Amaterasu fusion rig, which started recruiting from shrines after a meditating technician steadied the reactor. A Grey Lantern contractor once got inside its perimeter.

nodes.t: A medical startup whose recordings started running
nodes.x: It began by offering terminal patients a recording of their mind. For years the recordings did nothing. Then, in 2174, the first one started running (subject ███████ ██████, ██), and eleven of them now pilot the Choir.
nodes.z: The war · its halls under the Makassar pump works burn; what became of the recordings is unknown

nodes.t: Every program before a panel that can stop it
nodes.x: Created by Directive 10 when the Union's parliament learned, from UN footage, what Halden had sent into the Great Sand Sea in its name. Halden is its first case and Roland the only super it has approved. Its four hundred pages of conditions for a station on Mars become the Martian Research Directorate's founding law.

nodes.t: A supplier with no address
nodes.x: Appears in Joint Heavy Systems' depot records from 2181 as the consignee for HT-20 parts that never reached a Concord, and in a Navy procurement file as the supplier of a flight-weight fusion plant. Its directors are listed as ████████ ███ █████████. Congress has asked about it twice. Both answers were classified.

nodes.t: Care, not command
nodes.x: The people who keep the Jinn alive, with Khartoum's medical council behind them. They have learned to culture its tissue to heal burns. Their rule is that the Jinn is cared for, not commanded, and the raiders who stole four of their cultures never accepted it.

nodes.t: Pumps in Makassar, contracts in orbit
nodes.x: The front companies that buy what the Choir needs without anyone noticing, and have started selling continuity contracts to families in orbit. Nobody asked Beijing.
nodes.z: The war · silent after the Makassar Fire

nodes.t: The first improvised mechs outside any army
nodes.x: Mining companies that bolted steel plate onto legged construction walkers to escort copper convoys through militia country. Brannock-Hale's lawyers tried to stop the walker sales and failed.

nodes.t: Small elite teams, the best of every bloc
nodes.x: Began in 2172 as a four-pilot security firm holding a tin mine in Kivu for a mining consortium, paid in ore, and renamed itself the following year. It fields the best frame from each bloc, ships them in container ships under a different flag every year, and now rents out a super assembled from Concord parts.

nodes.t: Every container opened
nodes.x: After a Lantern Tender carried a giant through the canal, Panama began opening every container on every ship big enough to hide a frame. Every bloc protested and every bloc complied. In the war, the canal is taken.

nodes.s: A wandering survey station, inner Belt
nodes.t: Beijing's eyes travel with the caravans
nodes.x: A survey platform that Tianlong Orbital fits out for the Juno Concession and sends to wander the inner Belt, measuring drift, ore and the odd gravitational anomaly. Its forecasts tell the houses where to move and what to avoid, and they are good enough that no house turns one down. Its crews are Chinese scientists who like the Belt's freedom and hate its bookkeeping. Every forecast also goes home to Tianshu, and everyone in the Syndicate knows it. They take the forecasts anyway, and let the Array see what they want it to see.

EUX: Eurasian Pact · claimed by both halves

wS4: Desert supply routes, Jordan and Arabia
wS5: Great Sand Sea, Egypt and Libya
wE9: Eastern Europe, from the Baltic to the Black Sea
wW8: The Arctic archipelago, and the far south
wW16: Lake Superior to Hudson Bay, Canada

MINOR.t: Pirate crews take three tankers in a month
MINOR.x: Pirate crews seized three tankers in the strait in a single month. US carriers and Pact landing ships both arrived to escort shipping, and neither navy ever fully left. Japan paid for a regional coast guard instead. It was the first time it had bought calm rather than fought for it.

at: Salt flats of Bolivia, Chile and Argentina
MINOR.t: Two blocs bid for the battery metal
MINOR.x: The United States and the Union bid against each other for the salt flats' lithium. A coup attempt in Bolivia failed within days, and neither bloc ever admitted a role. Halcyon's whole battery bet rests on the supply contracts signed that winter. Brazil watched two blocs treat the continent as a quarry, and began looking across the Atlantic for partners who wouldn't.

MINOR.t: Mining walkers armoured against convoy raids
MINOR.x: Mining companies bolted steel plate onto legged construction walkers and used them to escort copper convoys through militia country. They were the first improvised mechs outside any bloc army. Brannock-Hale's lawyers tried to stop the walker sales and failed.

MINOR.t: US frames lent to a jungle counter-insurgency
MINOR.x: The United States lent two Garrison platoons to a Philippine counter-insurgency. Within a week the frames were mired to the knees, and insurgents with shoulder-fired rockets wrecked three of them. The Army quietly concluded that the Garrison was a frame for deserts and plains.

MINOR.t: A Tieniu crew walks its frame across the line
MINOR.x: A North Korean crew walked their export Tieniu across the DMZ and surrendered. Seoul handed it to the United States, whose engineers found the Iron Ox cruder than they had assumed and far harder to break.

MINOR.t: Turkey refuses frames on deck
MINOR.x: As the Pact built up forces for the Caspian, it asked to bring frame-carrying landing ships from its Baltic and Pacific fleets through the Bosporus and up the Volga–Don canal. Turkey refused anything with a mech on deck. The Pact fought the Caspian Crisis with the few landers already on the Caspian, and began building ground-effect craft there, which is why the Kaspiy exists.

MINOR.t: The first job for the firm that became Grey Lantern
MINOR.x: A mining consortium hired a small security firm whose four pilots had flown Garrisons for the US Army. They held a tin mine for eight months against three different militias and were paid in ore. The firm renamed itself Grey Lantern the following year.

MINOR.t: Export Tieshans guard a Pact-funded dam
MINOR.x: Tianlong engineering crews building a Pact-funded dam were guarded by export Tieshans. Downstream farmers blocked the river road for a month. Nobody fired, but every government in the region noticed whose frames were standing on the dam. That winter one company of the guards went unpaid and walked off into the Shan Hills, frames and all.

MINOR.t: Illegal logging crews fielding stolen walkers
MINOR.x: Illegal logging crews fielded stolen construction walkers and smuggled Tieniu under the canopy. Brazil bought a squadron of surplus Union Écuyers, whose quiet fuel cells and sensor heads found frames that helicopters flew straight over. Brasília has bought from Europe ever since, and increasingly sells to Africa.

MINOR.t: A rebel truce so the rescue frames can dig
MINOR.x: After a magnitude 8 earthquake, Japan sent Kizuna rescue frames by sea under the UN flag, and a UN envoy talked the government and a local insurgency into a truce so they could work. It held for ninety days, longer than either side expected.

MINOR.t: Tieshan-Kai frames set down on a disputed reef
MINOR.x: A Kaspiy-II landed a company of Tieshan-Kai on a disputed reef. Philippine and Vietnamese patrol boats circled it, and a Kestrel flight from a passing US carrier flew low overhead. Nobody fired. The frames are still there. Tianshu chose the reef.

MINOR.t: Black-market Haboobs against Lantern Customs
MINOR.x: Insurgents with Haboobs bought on the League black market fought for the gas fields against a government that had hired Grey Lantern. The Lantern Customs won most engagements and the insurgents won the war of attrition. The gas companies left first.

MINOR.t: Three weeks, second-hand frames on both sides
MINOR.x: A three-week border war fought entirely with second-hand frames: Bolivia's Pact-supplied Tieshans against Paraguay's rebuilt ex-US Garrisons. The Tieshans won on the open scrub and lost in the river marshes. Arms dealers from four blocs attended the ceasefire talks. Brazil hosted them, and seated a League delegation at the table: the first time an African bloc helped end a South American war. For a year afterwards, a white squad walked the ceasefire line through the marshes: the first UN frames either army trusted to watch a border.

MINOR.t: Every container ship searched for frames
MINOR.x: After a ship later identified as a Lantern Tender transited the canal, Panama began opening containers on every vessel big enough to hide a frame. Every bloc has protested and every bloc has complied. Shipping times have doubled, and Washington's planners have started calling it the canal problem.

MINOR.t: Rescuers arrive to find the work already done
MINOR.x: When floods cut off Palu, Japanese rescue crews landed three days later to find the town's buried streets already dug out. Survivors described a giant that worked through the night and walked into the sea at dawn. Vireo's shell companies had bought industrial pumps in Makassar a week earlier.

MINOR.t: Mexico signs a defence and industry pact with Washington
MINOR.x: Mexico signed a defence and industry agreement with the United States: a Brannock-Hale frame line in Monterrey, swap pits along the Gulf coast, and a joint command for the northern border. Mexico City calls it a partnership. Washington's planners call it strategic depth.

MINOR.t: The Pact's own road to orbit
MINOR.x: A forty-kilometre magnetic track climbing the Tian Shan, built to throw hull sections into orbit so the Pact never has to depend on a lunar slipway. Tianlong laid the track and Tianshu times the launches; OKB-7 builds the sections. Its first launch went up this year. Both General Staffs claim the rail, and it sits where their railways meet.

MINOR.t: A sealed car that knocked
MINOR.x: A sealed rail car left Geneva for Marseille under Union military escort. Its manifest read 'laboratory equipment, 60 t'. Railway staff were told not to look inside, and reported that it knocked. It was loaded onto a ship registered to ████████ ████████ and sailed for ██████. Three weeks later the Union was fighting in the Great Sand Sea.

MINOR.t: Three satellites, one flash, nobody's test
MINOR.x: Three bloc satellites recorded a double flash over an atoll in the central Pacific. The signature fits neither a bomb nor a launch. The United States, which administers the atoll, called it a meteor. The Navy closed the sea around it for a month, and when the sea reopened, the atoll's airstrip was eight hundred metres longer.

MINOR.t: Britain's leased frames go home to America
MINOR.x: Britain leased forty Sparrowhawks from Halcyon in 2164, maintained by Halcyon crews at Lakenheath. A year later Washington recalled them for the Tiltrotor Drops in Iran. They came back in 2166 worn out, with an invoice for the wear. Britain paid it under the Burden Share and started asking Vauclair-Ehrlich about sensors.

MINOR.t: Iceland is told afterwards
MINOR.x: The US Air Force built a Kestrel swap pit at Keflavik to cover the Greenland–Iceland gap, under the Burden Share's basing clause, and told Iceland's government when the first battery crane was already standing. The Althing passed a protest unanimously. Washington replied that the pit protected Iceland too, and billed it for the runway.

MINOR.t: Quebec stops selling south at Washington's price
MINOR.x: Quebec's hydrogen had gone south for twenty years at the price the Burden Share set. In 2176 a Montreal consortium signed a contract to supply the Union's fuel-cell depots at three times that price, and Ottawa let it stand. Washington called it a breach of the compact; Ottawa called it a market. The Union's BZ-4 stacks have run partly on Quebec hydrogen ever since, and the provinces that profited are the ones that vote for the Halifax Motion.

MINOR.t: Norway is billed for Svalbard
MINOR.x: A year after Svalbard, where the United States and the Union fought over Norway's own archipelago, Washington sent Oslo its share of the Harrier refit as a Burden Share cost of defending Norwegian waters. Norway paid. Its parliament also voted to buy its next frames from Boreal and its sensors from the Union, and to send an observer to Strasbourg.

MINOR.t: Water for Mexico, a parts plant for Brannock-Hale
MINOR.x: After the third drought year on the border, Washington offered Mexico a real share of the Colorado and the Rio Bravo, and a seat on the river commission, in return for joint border patrols and a Brannock-Hale parts plant in Coahuila. It was the first agreement in a century that newspapers on both sides called fair. Washington treats the neighbour it wants to keep better than the allies it thinks it already has, and it is why the Monterrey Accords take a week rather than a decade.
